places.chef: owner, chef · Kobe (Motomachi), Hyogo · Gyoza Taizo carries on a recipe that began in 1988, when its owner opened a small gyoza specialty shop called Furuya in Kobe. After more than thirty years of perfecting handmade dumplings in Hyogo, he brought that craft to Kyoto, reopening just off Kawaramachi in June 2020 under the new name Gyoza Taizo. It's an intimate, tucked-away counter spot on the second floor of the Shinobu Kaikan building, near Ura-Teramachi, with only about eight seats, so expect a cozy, made-to-order pace. · Wrap to order, not in advance. The owner makes each gyoza fresh once it's ordered so the thin dough keeps its crispness, even though it means a slower, small-batch rhythm. · Thin-skinned, made-to-order gyoza. The kitchen wraps each dumpling only after you order so the delicate skin stays crisp, then chars them and pairs them with a rich house miso dipping sauce (with optional Sichuan pepper). Fillings lean on Kagoshima black pork plus prominent domestic garlic and ginger, and fresh vegetables. places.chef: owner, chef · Imabari, Ehime Prefecture (Shikoku) — now in Kyoto · Mimatsu's roots reach back to 1950 in Imabari, on the udon-loving island of Shikoku, where the family's first shop opened under the name 三松 (Mimatsu). The second generation made the defining change that still shapes the bowls today: switching to meticulously made in-house noodles, a commitment so central that the shop was renamed 美松. The current owner is the third generation to carry the trade. A longtime Kyoto resident, they trained under the second-generation master back in Imabari before bringing the family's noodles to Kyoto, opening 麺処美松 in the Enmachi area in July 2019 and later settling near Kitano-Hakubaicho. Three generations on, the owner keeps refining the flavors little by little to suit how people eat today, while holding onto the foundations passed down from Imabari. · Stay true to the handmade-noodle craft handed down through three generations from Imabari, while gradually tuning the flavors to meet the tastes of today's diners. · Handmade udon with a soft, springy, mochi-like (モチモチ) bite — gentler than the sharp firmness of classic Sanuki udon — bathed in a broth built from kombu, bonito, and nibosh…

places.chef: Inoue Sadahiro (井上定博) · Owner, Chef · Demachiyanagi, Kamigyo-ku, Kyoto · Inoue no Gyoza is the second act of Inoue Sadahiro, the beloved owner-cook known around the neighborhood simply as "Demachi no occhan" (Demachi's uncle). For decades he ran the Gyoza no Ohsho branch in Demachi as its franchise owner and manager, becoming a local institution. When he reached the chain's mandatory retirement age, that branch closed at the end of October 2020 at age 70, to the regret of regulars. About two and a half years later, on March 3, 2023, he came back on his own terms, opening his own tiny counter shop, Inoue no Gyoza, right in the Demachi Masugata shopping arcade. It is a small spot of roughly nine counter seats where he cooks the same nostalgic town-Chinese food he is known for. · Inoue is famous for a standing offer he carried over from his Ohsho days: anyone genuinely short on money can eat their fill for free in exchange for washing dishes for 30 minutes afterward (for those 18 and over who are struggling). places.chef: Owner-operator, Cook · Mibu, Nakagyo-ku, Kyoto (near Nijo Station) · Ryuen has been grilling gyoza in the quiet, residential Mibu neighborhood west of Nijo Station since 1962, making it a genuine neighborhood institution loved by locals for more than 60 years. It is a small, unpretentious family operation, with counter seating wrapped around the kitchen so you watch everything happen in front of you. The kitchen is run by a trio of women: an older mother who works the grill, her daughter who hand-makes the gyoza, and a third member helping with service. A portrait of an earlier generation hangs on the wall, a quiet reminder of how long this family has been at it. What sets the shop apart is its hand-stretched skins (te-uchi no kawa), prepared so the dough comes out chewy and mochi-like rather than thin and crisp. The filling leans heavily on vegetables (cabbage in particular), with a moderate amount of ground meat and glass noodles, giving the gyoza a lighter, sweeter, umami-forward profile instead of a heavy, greasy one. Everything is made to order. The shop is firmly old-school: cash only, no reservations, Showa-era retro decor, and a reputation captured in one local description…

places.chef: Osamu Okuno (奥野修) · owner, roaster, singer-songwriter · Kyoto, Japan · Rokuyosha opened in 1950 at the Kawaramachi-Sanjo area, founded by Okuno Minoru after his family had run a coffee shop in Manchuria and returned home to Kyoto. The basement room came first; the ground floor was added in 1965 when bar service began. It has stayed a family business across three generations. The second-generation owner, Osamu Okuno, started working here around 1970 alongside family and still runs the basement room today. He is also known outside the shop as a singer-songwriter (Okuno Osamu). His son, the third-generation Kohei Okuno, joined the family business in 2013 after training for years at Maeda Coffee and running his own cafe in Higashiyama-Sanjo; he now mainly looks after the ground-floor kissaten while his father tends the basement. · Coffee roasted in-house and brewed cup by cup, in a quiet, timeless basement room where attentive, unhurried service lets guests linger. · Self-roasted, made-to-order coffee that is ground fresh and hand-dripped one cup at a time, with the basement leaning toward the deeper roasts. places.chef: Family-run okonomiyaki and yakisoba shop · Kyoto, Kita-ku, Tojiin Minami-cho (near Ritsumeikan University's Kinugasa campus) · Jambo (ジャンボ) has been a neighborhood okonomiyaki and yakisoba institution in Kyoto's Tojiin Minami-cho since 1974, sitting right in the student belt near Ritsumeikan University's Kinugasa campus and local schools. For decades it was the kind of place every student in the area knew by name - an affordable, fill-you-up shop run by a family that wanted young people and neighbors to be able to eat their fill. It built a fiercely loyal local following over more than 40 years, with regulars who have come back dozens of times, and its reputation eventually reached a national audience. In July 2018 the shop stopped offering dine-in service and moved to takeout only (you can order it pre-cooked or as raw batter to grill at home), but it has kept its signature flavor and its over-the-top portions intact. · Generosity above all - serving portions big enough to truly fill up students and neighbors at a price they can afford, which is the spirit the shop has carried since it opened. · Jambo lives up to its name: the okonomiyaki and yakisoba are famously enormous, routi…

places.chef: owner · Yamashina-ku, Kyoto (near Keihan Yamashina / Yamashina Station) · Kawamura is a small tonkatsu specialist tucked into Yamashina, on the eastern edge of Kyoto. It began as a humble shop called Jukuton (熟豚, later とんかつ食堂熟豚) before being reborn under the current name 熟成豚 かわむら. The whole shop is built around one idea: aged pork. The pork is selected by farmers and then entrusted to a carcass-aging specialist in Kyoto's Fushimi district, where it is dry-aged for roughly three to five weeks so its aroma and flavor deepen before it ever reaches the fryer. The room is small and bright, almost cafe-like, with just a handful of counter and table seats, and it tends to fill the moment the doors open, even on weekdays. Word has spread well beyond Kyoto, and the little shop has been recognized in the Michelin Guide's Bib Gourmand. · Let the pork speak. Rather than leaning on heavy sauce, the kitchen ages the meat to concentrate its natural umami and encourages diners to start with just the house-blend salt to taste the pork itself. · Tonkatsu made from dry-aged pork, double-fried for a crisp crust and tender, juicy interior

places.chef: Toshinori Sakakibara (榊原俊徳) · owner, head chef · Founded 1947 in Gion, Kyoto; later based in Ginza, Tokyo, and returned to Gion by the third generation (current location since around 1991) · Tempura Kyoboshi traces back to 1947, when it was founded in Gion; the shop later spent years in Ginza, Tokyo, and is now in the hands of its third-generation owner, Toshinori Sakakibara. His path to the counter was not gradual: he took over the family business at just 23 after his father fell ill, having trained at the long-established Tokyo tempura house Banhann. Under his stewardship the restaurant came back from Ginza to a quiet spot just east of Hanami-koji in Gion, where today only a handful of guests are welcomed each night at its small, roughly ten-seat counter. It is an intimate, single-counter room where the entire experience is built around watching one craftsman work the oil. · Sakakibara works in the old tradition that 'craftsmen learn by observation,' not by being told. He describes his trade as competing 'solely with tempura' and judges the oil by touch alone, reading its temperature from the feel of the cooking chopsticks, a craft he says is nearly impossible to put into words.…

places.chef: 市川 陽介 (Yosuke Ichikawa) · owner, roaster · 日本・京都 · 市川屋珈琲は、京都・東山の清水焼の窯元が集まっていた界隈に2015年に開いた喫茶店です。建物は店主・市川陽介さんの祖父がかつて営んでいた清水焼の工房兼住居で、市川さん自身もここで暮らしていました。築200年を数えるこの京町家はいったん取り壊しの話が持ち上がりましたが、市川さんは『この場所を残したい』という想いから、新築の約4倍という費用をかけて全面改修を決断。京町家作事組の手で、坪庭を望む大きな町家カフェとして生まれ変わりました。市川家は祖父・父ともに清水焼の陶芸家で、兄も焼物の道を継いでいます。市川さんだけは学生の頃から趣味で焙煎をするほどコーヒーを愛し、名門イノダコーヒで18年修業したのち、独立してこの店を開きました。 · 『一杯のコーヒーができること』を考え抜いた店づくり。市川さんは、来店した人がコーヒーを楽しむうちに自然と美しい器に出会えるよう、『一杯のコーヒーが、工芸への入り口に』なることを願っています。ネルドリップのなめらかで甘い一杯と、清水焼の器が、日常を少しだけ特別なものにしてくれます。 · 看板は、月ごとに移ろう旬のフルーツをふんわりした食パンとコクのある生クリームで挟んだ『季節のフルーツサンド』。果物の見極めや切り方、クリームの甘さの加減まで丁寧に仕立てられ、開店前から行列ができるほどの人気です。コーヒーは店内の焙煎機で日々自家焙煎し、ネルドリップでじっくり抽出。市川屋ブレンド・青磁ブレンド・馬町ブレンドの3種があり、それぞれ父や兄が手がけた清水焼のカップで供されます。市川屋ブレンドのカップは飲みやすさと保温性を考えて縁を薄く底を厚く、青磁ブレンドは香りが立つよう口を広く、と一杯ごとに器まで設計されています。卵サンドやデミオムライスといったメニューもあります。

places.chef: owner · Daitoku-ji, Kyoto · Izusen has served Kyoto's Buddhist vegetarian (shojin) cuisine since 1963 from a tranquil sub-temple, Daiji-in, within the grounds of Daitoku-ji — one of the head temples of Rinzai Zen. Guests dine looking out over a temple garden, eating from tetsubachi: round iron bowls that, in the Buddhist tradition, monks once carried to receive alms of food. · The kitchen follows the Zen ideal of three hearts: kishin (a joyful heart in cooking), roshin (a respectful heart that wastes nothing, attending to each grain of rice), and daishin (a compassionate, magnanimous heart). Tea-kaiseki (chakaiseki) is also served.

places.chef: Takahashi Sayaka · owner, baker · Kyoto, Japan · apelila is a 100% plant-based bakery and café tucked into the Takano neighborhood of Sakyo Ward, a short walk from Demachiyanagi station and Shimogamo Shrine, sitting along the river on Kawabata-dori. It was opened in 2015 by owner-baker Takahashi Sayaka, who had previously taught bread-making classes before turning her craft into a shop offering more than 20 kinds of bread. · Takahashi-san is reportedly not vegan herself; she chooses to bake entirely without animal-derived ingredients because she wants people to discover how delicious naturally-fermented yeast and simple, well-sourced ingredients can be. The shop leans on sustainability and quality: in-house milled Kyoto-grown whole wheat, organic dried fruit, and a decades-old starter. · Naturally-leavened vegan breads and baked goods made with a house-milled Kyoto whole-wheat flour and a sourdough starter that has been continuously fed for roughly two decades; plus a café lunch headlined by a vegan cheeseburger plate with a chickpea patty and fermented soy yogurt, alongside donuts, melon bread, caramel cream pastries, cookies and waffles.

places.chef: owner · 一乗寺, Sakyo Ward, Kyoto · Opened in 2011 on Ichijoji's famous "Ramen Street" (ラーメン街道) in Kyoto's Sakyo Ward, Menya Gokkei staked out its own corner of one of Japan's most competitive ramen districts. The name 極鶏 ("Gokkei") fuses 極 (extreme/perfected) with 鶏 (chicken), and the shop has stayed laser-focused on a single idea ever since. · A one-bowl, one-idea shop: rather than chase variety, Gokkei pours everything into perfecting a single, unmistakable chicken broth — its own self-described 'one-of-a-kind soup to savor.' · The signature 極鶏 鶏だく: an ultra-concentrated chicken paitan so thick it is often described as 'doro-kei' (muddy) and famously dense enough that a spoon can stand upright in it. Chicken carcasses are simmered to an extreme, near-pottage consistency to create what the shop calls a 'soup you eat rather than drink.' Variations build on the same base: 赤だく (fiery red chili), 黒だく (fragrant black mayu garlic oil), and 魚だく (a fish-infused twist).
places.gfd: Not celiac-safe. The ramen is built on wheat noodles, and the ultra-thick chicken broth is seasoned with a soy-sauce-based tare (Japanese shoyu almost always contains wheat). No gluten-free noodle or gluten-free preparation is offered, and the kitchen is a single-concept ramen shop with no dedicated allergen handling. Diners requiring strict gluten avoidance cannot eat safely here.
places.vgd: Not vegan. The entire menu is anchored on an ultra-concentrated chicken (paitan) broth made by simmering chicken carcasses to a near-pottage consistency, plus chicken-based toppings (鶏だく = extra chicken). There is no plant-based broth or vegan bowl. Vegetarians and vegans cannot be accommodated.
places.hours: 11:30–22:00 (Tue–Sun); closed Mon plus irregular days off. Ends when the soup runs out, so it may close early even within stated hours.

places.chef: owner-operator · Kyoto · Shinpuku Saikan began life in 1938 as a humble street stall (yatai) near Kyoto Station and has grown into one of the founding names of Kansai ramen. The honten (main shop) still stands on Higashi-Shiokoji Street by the Takabashi crossing, a short walk from Kyoto Station, and remains a cash-only, family-run institution that locals and travelers line up for. · Captured in the shop's own line — roughly, 'a bowl that makes you want to eat it again and again' — the focus is on that one addictive, instantly recognizable black broth rather than menu breadth. · Its signature is chuka soba in a startlingly jet-black, deeply colored soy-sauce broth built on a chicken- and pork-bone base — the original 'Kyoto Black.' Despite the intense dark appearance, regulars describe the soup as surprisingly mild, clean, and easy to drink, which is why it doubles as a beloved asa-ra (morning ramen) from the 9:00 opening. The pork-fat fried rice (yakimeshi), often ordered alongside a small bowl, is nearly as famous as the noodles.

places.chef: owner-operator · A small ramen-ya near Gojo in Kyoto's Shimogyo ward, a stretch close to Kyoto Station that has surprisingly few standout eateries, which helped Kubota stand out and draw a steady mix of locals and international visitors. The dining room is intimate — roughly ten counter seats divided by partitions, a layout regulars liken to a see-through version of the famous solo-booth chains. · The cooking leans into a made-to-order ideal — the noodles are boiled fresh to order — prioritizing texture and the quality of the noodle itself over speed or piling on toppings. · The house signature is the ginjo miso tsukemen: thick, glossy, springy noodles — often compared to Sanuki udon for their substance and chew — served with a rich, grainy-textured miso dipping broth layered with seafood umami and ground pork, finished with a hint of chili-oil spice that some have likened to Kansai-style spice curry. A ginjo shoyu (chicken-soy) ramen rounds out the lineup, with a marinated egg and rice-bowl sides as add-ons.
places.gfd: No gluten-free options. Not suitable for celiac or strict gluten avoidance. No allergen menu or dedicated gluten-free handling is advertised.

places.chef: 西岡津世志 (Nishioka Tsuyoshi) · founder, chef · Kyoto · Founded in October 2006 in the student town of Ichijoji, this is widely regarded as the pioneer of Kansai-style Jiro ramen. Founder Nishioka Tsuyoshi apprenticed in the Ramen Marji lineage (itself descended from the legendary Ramen Jiro in Tokyo), serving as branch manager at Marji's Nishi-Arai shop before opening his own counter here. places.chef: owner-chef · Kyoto (Emmachi / Nishinokyo, Nakagyo-ku) · A small, quietly run ramen counter a few minutes from JR Emmachi station, kept deliberately modest: just nine seats along an L-shaped counter, worked by the owner and one assistant. places.chef: ramen shop, tsukemen specialist · Kyoto · 麺や高倉二条 is the head shop of a small, tightly run Kyoto ramen family that also includes the Sugari shops and a couple of sibling counters. The shops are deliberately low-key: the storefront carries almost no signage — just a small wooden nameplate on a stylish, machiya-like facade — so from the street it reads more like a quiet townhouse than a ramen joint, and it fills mostly by word of mouth. · The group cooks under the banner of 医食同源 (ishoku-dogen) — 'food and medicine share one source' — aiming for bowls that nourish as much as they satisfy, presented with an understated, distinctly Kyoto restraint. · The signature is a rich tonkotsu-gyokai (pork-bone and dried-fish/bonito) bowl, served as both ramen and the group's celebrated tsukemen. The dipping broth combines long-simmered pork bones with niboshi and katsuobushi dashi, balanced toward a deep finish; the noodles are house-made, flat and silky (with a yuzu-noodle option), and the prized topping is motsu (offal), alongside char-pork and wagyu choices.

places.chef: 田口有司（Taguchi Yuji） · Long-established Kyoto ramen institution, Pre-dawn opening near Kyoto Station · Kyoto Station / Takabashi, Shimogyo-ku · Born in 1947 near Kyoto Station at the spot locals call "Takabashi," this is the original shop of the celebrated Daiichi Asahi lineage of Kyoto ramen. It started life as a humble eatery (Asahi Shokudo / 旭食堂) and was renamed 第一旭 in 1956 as it became a dedicated ramen specialist, opening before dawn to feed early-morning workers and travelers near the station — a habit that survives today in its famous 6 a.m. opening. · A long-protected, continually refined old-school taste ("守り続け、磨き続けてきた老舗の味") built on careful sourcing — Kyoto-grown Kujo negi and mung-bean sprouts, raw soy sauce from a long-established Kyoto (Fushimi) maker, and char siu from a single specific grade of domestic pork chosen for its lean, clean balance of fat and meat so the soup stays gentle on the palate. · The signature 特製ラーメン (chuka soba): a clear yet deeply savory pork-bone broth seasoned with raw Kyoto soy sauce, piled with thinly sliced char siu, a generous tangle of Kujo green onions, and bean sprouts, over medium-thick dried-aged wheat noodles.

places.chef: Sodeoka (袖岡) · owner, chef · Kyoto · The shop's name とうひち is written 藤七 and read 'touhichi' in the Kyoto dialect. After leaving a corporate career in his late 30s, the owner (Sodeoka) trained for about four years at the renowned Kyoto ramen house 京都千丸しゃかりき (Kyoto Senmaru Shakariki) before opening his own counter in a quiet residential pocket of Kita Ward in March 2015. In April 2022 he relocated the shop to its current spot a short walk from Shugakuin Station, into premises that had previously housed his sister shop Suguru. · A restrained, transparency-first aesthetic: a simple-looking but deeply layered broth meant to slide cleanly across the palate, with the raw-pressed-soy-sauce chicken-clear style being the direction the owner settled on during his training years. · The signature bowl is the tori-shoyu raa-men: a crystal-clear chicken broth (tori-seitan) seasoned with raw-pressed nama-age soy sauce and gilded with fragrant chicken oil, topped with two kinds of chashu, thick menma and chopped green onion. The repertoire also runs to a richer tori-paitan, a niboshi (sardine) seafood bowl, and tsuke-soba dipping noodles served with a kombu-steeped water bath for the noodles.

places.chef: owner-operator · Hokuriku (Ishikawa/Fukui) origins; established in Kyoto Ichijoji in 2011. · Ikedaya began life outside Kyoto, in the Hokuriku region (its first shop was in Nonoichi, Ishikawa), before the owner brought the shop to Kyoto's Ichijoji district in 2011. places.chef: owner-operated counter tsukemen shop · Kyoto (Nakagyo-ku, Rokkaku-dori / Shinkyogoku) · A small, tucked-away tsukemen specialist on Rokkaku-dori in the Shinkyogoku/Teramachi shopping warren, just a short walk from Shijo-Kawaramachi and Kyoto City Hall-mae Station. places.chef: Tatsuo Uemura (上村) · owner, chef · Kyoto, Japan (Shimogyo-ku, near Shijo-Karasuma) · Born in 1954, Uemura worked for a fish company before moving to Kansai and running several restaurants. He briefly closed early on to refine his recipe after realizing Kyoto's hot, humid summer (the shop opened in August) shifted customers' taste away from the cold-northern, heavily-salted style he had trained in. · Uemura rejects a profit-first approach, saying he doesn't think of ramen as a money-making tool and prioritizing quality over margin. places.chef: Sasaki Koji · owner-chef, family-run kitchen · Kyoto (Gion lineage, Beijing-style Chinese cuisine) · Seikatei opened in 1982 in the quiet temple district near Ginkaku-ji. Its roots run back to 盛京亭 (Seikyotei), a Beijing-style restaurant founded in 1951 in the heart of Gion's hanamachi (geisha district). The founder's father served as head chef at Seikyotei, and the son went on to open this independent shop, carrying most of the original menu with it. · A Kyoto take on Chinese food: because the original Gion shop cooked for geiko and refined patrons, it deliberately dialed back heavy aromatics like garlic and excess oil. Seikatei keeps that restraint — light white-pressed soybean oil (shirashime-yu), local Matsui-brewery sake instead of cooking wine, and clean, delicate flavors over punch. · Goma-gyoza (sesame dumplings): roasted sesame is kneaded right into the wrapper, with a filling of only cabbage, Chinese chives, pork and sake, then pan-fried in a heavy cast iron pan until the surface turns crisp. places.chef: owner · Kyoto — Gion / Higashiyama · にぼ魂 opened on August 8, 2025 in the heart of Gion, just north of Gion-Shijo Station off Nawate-dori, taking over a space that had until then housed a kasu-udon shop (かすうどん). places.chef: owner-chef · Kyoto (lineage from Daiei Ramen, Minami ward) · The original Ramen Daiei was founded in 1980 in Kyoto's Minami ward. places.vgd: Not a vegan-friendly stop. places.chef: owner, chef · Kyoto (Takano / Ichijoji, Sakyo-ku) · Ramen Viska opened on July 14, 2023, in a quiet residential pocket behind Takano Post Office, on the fringe of Ichijoji's famously crowded ramen battleground. It is a true one-person shop: the owner cooks, serves, and chats single-handedly. The space is a renovated former snack bar with a glossy high bar-style counter of about five seats, and the owner greets guests in a suit and tie rather than the usual ramen-cook garb. There is no noren curtain out front. · A minimalist, single-minded devotion to tonkotsu done well — quality broth over a broad menu, served personally and explained in detail to anyone curious. · Super-rich kotteri tonkotsu: a pork-bone broth simmered until thick enough that, as locals joke, the spoon could stand up in it, yet it stays mild and clean on the palate with no porky funk, drinking almost like a potage. The lineup is deliberately spare — kotteri (rich), assari (a remarkably clear, transparent tonkotsu, finished with yuzu zest), a Bisuro (ビス郎) bowl, and tsukemen — paired with medium-straight noodles and well-seasoned roast-pork chashu. The focus is entirely the bowl.
places.gfd: This is a wheat-noodle tonkotsu shop with no gluten-free offering. The noodles are wheat, the tare is almost certainly wheat-based shoyu, and the menu (kotteri/assari/tsukemen) is built around standard ramen components. No celiac-safe option and no published allergen handling. Not suitable for anyone requiring strict gluten avoidance.
places.vgd: Every bowl is built on a pork-bone (tonkotsu) broth and topped with roast-pork chashu; there is no vegetable or vegan broth and no meat-free option on the menu. Not suitable for vegans or vegetarians.

places.chef: owner · Kyoto · Kyogame occupies a restored Kyoto machiya townhouse along Imadegawa-dori, a short walk from Demachiyanagi. The owner, known affectionately as Kame-san, runs it less like a polished restaurant and more like a friend's home — courtyard garden, tatami rooms where you can stretch your legs, and the unhurried feel of an old popular izakaya. · Generous, unfussy, and deliberately affordable — the lunch bowls are priced so that students and regulars can come often, in a room meant to feel like dropping by someone's house rather than dining out. · The house centerpiece is a hearty garlic motsunabe: select beef offal in a quality chicken-bone broth, offered in white-miso, soy, or salt versions, alongside other izakaya sides. places.chef: owner · Kyoto (originally Uzumasa / west Kyoto) · Sugichiyo is the revival of a legendary Kyoto ramen shop. The original opened in 1999 in the Uzumasa area of western Kyoto and drew daily lines for roughly a decade before it closed at the end of 2009 — reportedly because the crowds it attracted had become difficult to sustain. After about twelve years dormant, the name returned in June 2021 in a renovated spot down a Takase River alley just west of Shijo-Kawaramachi, in the heart of central Kyoto's nightlife district. The current team is said to have inherited the complete original recipe directly from the founder. · Faithfully carry forward a beloved recipe rather than reinvent it — a nostalgic, unpretentious bowl served with quiet, courteous hospitality instead of the high-intensity style of many modern ramen shops. · Chashu ramen — the bowl that built the shop's reputation. places.chef: independent neighborhood Chinese / noodle house, keeper of the 鳳舞系 からしそば tradition · Kyoto (北区 紫野, on Horikawa near Kitaoji) · 鳳飛 is part of Kyoto's celebrated 鳳舞系 — the lineage of Chinese cooks who trained under master 高華吉, a Cantonese immigrant, at the legendary 鳳舞, which opened in 1967 and closed, much mourned, in 2009. 高 is remembered as a pioneer of Kyoto-style Chinese cooking who reworked Chinese food for local palates into something light, restrained and broth-forward — chicken- and kombu-based, with the oil and aggressive aromatics pulled back. places.chef: Noriko Fujita (藤田典子) · owner, chef · Kyoto · The owner spent years as a hospital nurse, earning her nursing credentials while raising her family and returning to study around age 38 after her children grew more independent. Working grueling night shifts, she found that a bowl of ramen eaten after coming off a night shift restored both her stamina and her spirit. That comfort became a calling: at 53 she set out to open her own shop. · She refused to cut corners with wholesale noodles, investing in a professional noodle machine (from Daikoku Manufacturing, around 2.7 million yen) so she could make her own noodles in-house, because she wants customers to taste the difference of truly handmade noodles. Sitting near the universities, she also wants to send students and young people off well-fed and happy, an extension of her caretaking instincts from nursing into feeding her community. · Jiro-style ramen with generous pork and vegetable toppings; the signature is the 小豚ラーメン (kobuta / small-pork ramen). Bowls are customized at order time by noodle quantity and the classic Jiro toppings of garlic, extra vegetables, and oil.

places.chef: family-run neighborhood shokudo · Kyoto (Meiji-era Sarashina lineage out of Shinkyogoku) · Sarashina traces its roots to a Meiji-era soba house centered on a main shop in Kyoto's Shinkyogoku shopping district; this Shogoin branch grew out of that lineage and today runs as its own quiet, independent neighborhood shokudo. You find it by walking some ten meters down a covered alley barely a meter wide — easy to stroll right past — until a low old-fashioned door opens onto a small room of rustic, folk-craft furnishings and a single mat of raised tatami seating that feels unchanged for decades. · Unfussy, neighborly cooking: an old soba shokudo that quietly serves nostalgic chuka-soba and home-style donburi at gentle prices, prizing warmth and consistency over trend. · The bowl regulars come for is the chuka-soba: pale, straight-cut Chinese noodles in a gentle, light broth that carries a subtly Japanese, dashi-leaning character rather than the heavy richness of a modern ramen-ya. places.gfd: Everything central here is wheat-based: the chuka-soba noodles are Chinese wheat noodles, the soba/udon are wheat-containing, and the bowls feature wheat-gluten fu (umefu and dried fu) plus a Japanese-style broth that almost certainly relies on wheat-containing shoyu. places.vgd: This is a traditional soba/udon shokudo whose dishes center on fish-and-meat dashi, pork chashu, kamaboko fish cake, and donburi over rice. There is no vegan offering; a vegan diner would have essentially nothing safe here.

places.chef: owner-chef · Kyoto · The owner came up through two pillars of Kyoto's back-fat ramen tradition: he trained at the legendary Shinpuku Saikan and then served as manager (tencho) at Chinyu in Ichijoji before striking out on his own. The shop opened on November 1, 2021, in a quiet residential pocket of Minami-ku's Yoshoin district, taking over a former ramen storefront. · To serve honest, old-school Kyoto ramen (昔ながらの京都ラーメン) at neighborhood prices: the bolder, back-fat-forward seasoning that south-Kyoto locals favor, paired with the snappy medium-thin noodles that define the city's style. It is built as an approachable, family-friendly local shop rather than a destination. · The signature is a classic back-fat soy-sauce bowl (背脂醤油ラーメン) on a robustly seasoned chicken-based broth, finished with green onion, two slices of chashu, and menma. The kitchen also runs a back-fat mazesoba and a chicken bowl, plus hearty sides — beef-tendon rice bowls, karaage, and ginger-pork sets — and weekend morning ramen service.
places.gfd: No gluten-free options. There is no indication of gluten-free menu items or accommodation, and the kitchen shares boiling water and surfaces with wheat noodles. A celiac or strict gluten-free diner cannot eat safely here.
places.vgd: Not vegan-friendly. The core bowls are built on chicken and pork (back-fat) broth with chashu (pork), and the shop also serves beef-tendon rice bowls, karaage, and ginger-pork sets. No plant-based broth or vegan ramen is offered. Vegans cannot be accommodated.

places.chef: owner/operator (same team as 貝だし麺きた田) · Kyoto — sister shop to 貝だし麺きた田 near Kyoto Station; this branch sits in the Jurakukai/Senbon-Marutamachi neighborhood near Nijo Station. · Kawano is the younger sibling of 貝だし麺きた田, the popular shellfish-broth noodle shop just north of Kyoto Station. When the team opened this second place near Nijo Station in February 2025, they deliberately did not repeat the shellfish formula — they set out to 'try something unconventional, with a Japanese sensibility,' and chose duck as their canvas. · Restraint and refinement over heavy ramen convention — the kitchen treats the duck like washoku, controlling temperature and timing so the meat stays tender and pink, and lets the broth deepen as the noodles slowly release into it. · Kamo soba (duck noodles): a clear, delicate duck broth made from just duck and water, served over Hokkaido wheat noodles and topped with low-temperature duck loin, white and green scallion, and bamboo shoots, finished with duck fat. Variations include duck-and-shellfish Chinese noodles (shoyu or shio), duck mazesoba, and duck tsukemen, plus duck rice and duck-yukhoe bowls.
places.gfd: Not gluten-free. places.chef: 古山智浩 (Tomohiro Furuyama) · owner, founder · Kyoto (Saiin) · Jinrai opened its Saiin flagship on February 2, 2012, right by Saiin station, and grew from this single counter into a small Kyoto-area group of six shops (Ichijoji, Aeon Mall locations, the Kyoto Racecourse stand, and Aeon Mall Takanohara in Kizugawa). Despite the expansion, the Saiin honten remains the original neighborhood ramen-ya that built the name. · The owner frames running the shop as 'enjoying the business' — treating service as a kind of friendly competition where staff read each customer and move as one unified team to keep the line moving and the bowls hot. · The signature bowl is a soy-sauce-based chicken-and-pork-bone ramen with a layer of aromatic back-fat (seabura) floating on top — rich and kotteri but described by regulars as surprisingly easy to drink. It is finished with Kyoto's traditional Kujo negi and house-made chashu and menma, on thin, springy custom wheat noodles made to order by the respected noodle maker Menya Teikaku. places.chef: owner-chef · Kyoto (Kamigamo / Kita Ward) · Menya Shourin opened on February 10, 2020 in the leafy Kamigamo district of Kyoto's Kita Ward, just north of Kamigamo Shrine near Kyoto Sangyo University. The owner trained at the well-known Kyoto ramen group Kirameki no Tori (キラメキノトリ) before striking out on his own. · Careful broth-making aimed at a rich umami with no off-flavors (雑味のない、まろやかな味), served in a clean, café-like space welcoming to students, families and locals. · The signature bowl is the niku-paitan soba (肉白湯そば) — an emulsified chicken-and-pork-bone (鶏豚骨) white broth that is full-bodied yet clean and mellow, finished with coarse black pepper. A special chicken paste is meant to be stirred in partway through to deepen the flavor. Straight, medium-thin noodles come from the respected Teigaku (棣鄂) noodle maker. places.vgd: Every bowl is built on an animal base — a rich emulsified chicken-and-pork-bone (鶏豚骨) white broth, with meat toppings and a chicken paste stirred in mid-meal. There are no vegan or vegetarian ramen options; sides include fried chicken and rice. No plant-based menu noted.

places.chef: owner-chef · Garamon began life not as a ramen shop but as a charcoal-grill yakitori izakaya called 炭焼賀ら茂ん (Sumiyaki Garamon). Tucked into a quiet residential block south of Misonobashi near Kamigamo, it later changed its business format to a ramen shop while keeping the same name and its shoes-off, lived-in izakaya feel. · An owner-run, single-counter shop designed so one person can comfortably walk in and eat well for cheap; quiet, residential, no-frills, with the kitchen's attention going into the dashi-forward broth and the seared pork rather than spectacle. · Two bowls anchor the menu, both at the same modest price: a lighter 中華そば (chuka soba) and a richer 背脂醤油 (sebabura shoyu) with back-fat and added oil. The broth blends pork bone, chicken carcass, kombu and seafood, leaning unusually far toward a Japanese dashi character so that it edges toward udon/soba territory while keeping ramen body and sweetness. The signature topping is a thick slice of aburi (seared) chashu, individually torched and brushed with glaze for aroma.
places.gfd: This is a traditional chuka soba / seb-abura shoyu ramen shop. The bowls are built on wheat noodles and a soy-sauce (shoyu) tare, which in Japan is almost always brewed with wheat, over a pork-bone, chicken, kombu and seafood broth. No gluten-free noodles, tare, or accommodations are mentioned in any source, and there is no indication the kitchen handles celiac-level allergen requests. Not suitable for anyone needing to avoid gluten.
places.vgd: The signature bowls are built on a pork-bone, chicken and seafood (fish/kombu) broth and are topped with seared chashu pork. There are no vegan or vegetarian ramen options described anywhere; the menu centers on animal-based broths and meat toppings.

places.chef: owner-operator · Ichijoji, Sakyo Ward, Kyoto · Arajin opened on September 10, 2014, on a corner of the Ichijoji intersection — one of Kyoto's most intensely competitive ramen districts. It is a compact, clean, counter-only shop (about 12 seats) run as essentially a one-person operation, where guests buy a ticket from the machine before ordering. · The cooking leans on careful craftsmanship — a broth made rich without becoming heavy, and medium-thick, hand-kneaded-style noodles specially ordered from an established noodle maker for good chew and slurp. The result is described as crave-worthy and habit-forming. · The signature bowl is the rich miso tonkotsu ramen (濃厚味噌豚骨ラーメン): a creamy, full-bodied pork-bone broth carrying the depth and aroma of miso, finished with back fat, and rounded out with green onion, thin-sliced chashu, half a seasoned egg, nori, menma, and sesame. A shoyu tonkotsu version is the other pillar of the menu.

places.chef: owner · A neighborhood ramen counter tucked near the Hyakumanben crossing west of Kyoto University, Takumi has been feeding locals and students for close to two decades. It is the kind of unpretentious machi-chuka spot you slip into for a satisfying, affordable bowl, including late at night. · Comfort over flash: carefully drawn-out broth, an almost extravagant amount of negi, and a friendly counter feel that has kept regulars coming back for years. · The signature is the Takumi Chashu-men: a bowl piled with thin slices of chashu pork arranged like overflowing flower petals, set over a long-simmered pork-bone (tonkotsu) soy-sauce broth that is at once viscous and mellow, without any heavy or off-putting edge. A generous heap of Kujo-style green onion crowns the bowl, cutting the richness so it eats clean and bright. A lighter, clear shoyu chuka-soba is also offered for those who want something more delicate.
places.gfd: This is a traditional chuka-soba (ramen) shop: wheat noodles in a pork-bone/soy-sauce broth, with a wheat-based shoyu tare. There is no indication of any gluten-free noodle, dedicated equipment, or allergen handling. A celiac or strictly gluten-free diner cannot safely eat the ramen here, and nothing on the menu (ramen, tsukemen, gyoza) is gluten-free. Treat as not suitable.

places.chef: 相場哲夫 (Tetsuo Aiba) · Kyoto-Chinese restaurant, からしそば specialist, 鳳舞 (Houmai) lineage · Kyoto (Kamigyō-ku, Imadegawa) · 鳳舞楼 carries forward one of Kyoto's most beloved culinary lineages: that of 鳳舞 (Houmai), the legendary Kyoto-Chinese restaurant opened by chef 高華吉 (Kō Kakichi) in 1967 and closed in 2009, within whose walls generations of Kyoto families held their celebrations. Kyoto-style Chinese itself traces back further, to 支那料理ハマムラ (Hamamura), the city's first Chinese restaurant, opened in Gion in 1924 by 濱村保三; it was there that Kō Kakichi honed the approach of lightening Chinese dishes with Japanese dashi to suit Kyoto's refined, geisha-district palate before founding his own 鳳舞. places.chef: 芥川 (Akutagawa) · owner, founder · Yokohama iekei lineage via Ramen Musashi-ya (ラーメン武蔵屋) · Founder Akutagawa and his colleague Hirayama (who became a later shop owner) met working at Ramen Musashi-ya, the parent shop in the iekei (家系) tradition. The two set out to bring real Yokohama-style iekei ramen to Kyoto, scouring the city by bicycle until they found the spot on Imadegawa, just east of the Hyakumanben intersection by Kyoto University's main gate, opening on September 8, 2018. · Keep it honest and accessible: Akutagawa held the bowl to the parent shop's price point even as he sourced ingredients carefully, absorbing higher costs through tight management so students and locals could afford a serious bowl. He framed the work around how much he could give back to customers. · The standard bowl (並ラーメン) of rich pork-and-chicken-bone tonkotsu-shoyu broth, built iekei-style by continuously replenishing the stock (継ぎ足し). It comes with thick noodles, thick-cut pork loin chashu, spinach, and sheets of nori, with free bean-sprout namul and refillable rice on the side. Diners are asked their preferences for noodle firmness, broth strength, and back fat.

places.chef: second-generation owner · Yamashina, Kyoto · Yonakiya is one of the old guard of Kyoto ramen, a shop that has stood along the Nara-kaido road in the Otsuka district of Yamashina for decades and is treated as one of the originals of the city's ramen lineage. It was founded by the previous master and has since passed to the next generation, who carries on the same single-bowl tradition. · A one-bowl shop in the truest sense: it does essentially one thing, the old Kyoto chuka soba, and has done it the same way long enough that decades of consistency on a single corner are taken as proof of the cooking. · Chuka soba: relatively thin, springy straight noodles in a soy-based broth drawn from pork bone and chicken (豚骨・鶏ガラ), topped with sweet pork back-fat (背脂) that floats on the surface. The clean, delicate dashi is carried by the strength of the soy tare, so a bowl that looks rich eats surprisingly light. The shop is known for slicing its big chashu fresh to order.
places.gfd: A classic wheat-noodle chuka soba: the noodles are wheat, the soy tare is almost certainly wheat-based shoyu, and the broth uses pork and chicken. No gluten-free menu, no published allergen handling, and no indication of any wheat-free preparation. Not safe for a celiac diner.
places.vgd: This is a traditional Kyoto chuka-soba shop whose single signature bowl is built on a pork-bone and chicken (豚骨・鶏ガラ) broth finished with sweet pork back-fat (背脂) and a soy tare. The menu centers on this one animal-based ramen, so there is no vegan option. A plant-based diner cannot eat here.
places.hours: Tuesday-Friday 11:00-15:00; closed Monday, Saturday, Sunday. Closes early when the day's noodles/ingredients run out. Note: some guides list a longer through-service window of 11:00-18:00 until sell-out; the shop sells out frequently, so arriving early is advised.

places.chef: 木村勉 (Tsutomu Kimura) · founder · Kyoto · This is the sohonten — the original headquarters — of Tenkaippin, the cult chicken-broth ramen chain that began in Kyoto. In November 1971, founder Tsutomu Kimura, having lost his job when the gallery company he worked for went bankrupt, had a friend build him a ramen cart out of scrap metal and started pulling a yatai (food cart) around the Ginkaku-ji area. On opening night he reportedly sold only 11 bowls. He kept experimenting, and after three years and nine months he perfected the now-legendary kotteri broth. With the goodwill of a stone-mason whose lot he was using, the cart was fixed in place and grew into his first storefront in August 1975 — on this Ichijoji site, which remains the chain's spiritual home. · Kimura's idea was a broth that is 'eaten, not drunk' — a slow-cooked chicken-and-vegetable kotteri so concentrated it behaves like a sauce. The beef-tendon special was developed personally by the chairman over many trial batches, balancing the sweet-savory tendon to harmonize with that signature soup, and the recipe is kept exclusive to the sohonten. · The signature is the kotteri (こってり) bowl: a thick, almost potage-like broth si…

No gluten-free noodles, broth, or accommodation is offered, and there is no dedicated fryer. A celiac diner cannot eat the ramen here.
places.vgd: Not suitable for vegans. The signature broth is a long-simmered chicken-bone (鶏ガラ) and vegetable kotteri base, and the flagship-only specials are beef-tendon (牛すじ) ramen and pork rice (豚重). There are no plant-based broth, noodle, or topping options.

places.chef: owner-chef · Kyoto · A husband-and-wife team who began as a pop-up in the Fukakusa area, running for about three months before opening this permanent shop near Toji Station in January 2021, taking over a former Chinese-restaurant space in Minami Ward. The couple draw on their own experience raising children to run a warm, family-friendly counter. · The name itself is the philosophy: to thoroughly and patiently slow-simmer the chicken. The owners describe themselves as still refining the recipe, treating the bowl as a work in continual improvement. · An exceptionally concentrated chicken paitan (torigara hakutou) — the signature 'Tokoton Tori'. Chicken and a generous amount of vegetables are simmered thoroughly and gently for a long time (the literal meaning of the shop's name) into a broth so thick a ladle can stand upright in it. It is rich in collagen — enough that it sets when cooled — yet the vegetables keep the finish surprisingly clean rather than heavy. Flat noodles from Kyoto noodle maker Teikaku cling to the dense soup; sets pair the bowl with a donburi of house-made chashu, scallion, egg yolk and fried-onion shrimp oil, and fish-powder, chili and mazesoba variations are …

places.chef: owner-chef · Opened in 2020 in the Kuze district of Kyoto's Minami-ku, on the edge of Mukou City near JR Mukomachi Station. · Before opening his own shop, the owner spent roughly ten years training at one of Kyoto's most storied ramen institutions, Shinpuku Saikan (新福菜館) at Takabashi — the legendary home of jet-black soy chuka soba. He carries that Kyoto rich-soy lineage forward while adding his own refinements. · All vegetables and ingredients are domestically sourced, and the broth itself is the product of constant tinkering — described on the shop's own site as a rich-soy soup 'developed through improvement upon improvement' to land on a deep flavor with a light, clean finish. · The flagship bowl is the 醤油中華そば (rich-soy chuka soba), a concentrated pork-bone-and-soy broth that drinks surprisingly clean, finished with Kyoto's prized Kujo green onions. Other draws include the 宇宙一のまぜそば ("best-in-the-universe" maze soba), 濃厚担々麺, the vegetable-laden 京都タンメン, and a much-loved fried-rice set.
places.gfd: This is a traditional Kyoto-style rich-soy chuka soba shop. No gluten-free menu, no gluten-free noodles, and no published allergen accommodation. Not suitable for anyone requiring strict celiac-level avoidance of wheat.
places.vgd: Every signature bowl is built on an animal foundation: a rich pork-bone and soy broth, topped with chashu (pork). There are no published plant-based options.

places.chef: owner · Kyoto, Sakyo-ku (Seigoin / near Kumano Shrine) · Despite carrying the famous Daiichi Asahi name, this Kumano shop is not part of the celebrated honke (head shop) founded in 1947 by Kyoto Station's Takabashi. It is a survivor of an old chain expansion: when the original franchising company folded, individual shops like this one carried on independently, keeping the name and the recipes they had been built around. A yellowed signboard from that era — roughly four decades old — still hangs out front, a tangible piece of Kyoto ramen history. · An unpretentious, value-driven neighborhood ramen-ya: hearty, chashu-forward bowls under 1,000 yen in a retro counter setting that locals have leaned on for years. · A Kyoto-style chuka soba: a pork-bone broth that reads surprisingly light and clean despite its richness, carrying a soy tare and a faint sheen of back-fat in the classic Kyoto manner. Bowls come piled with generous chashu — diners can choose leaner thigh or richer belly cuts — over medium-thin straight noodles, with bean sprouts, scallion and a soft egg. Spicy miso can be stirred in partway through to shift the flavor.

places.chef: ramen shop, sister brand of Ramen Mugyu · Kyoto (Nishikyo Ward) · Stamen (stylized START WITH MEN) opened in January 2023 in the Kashihara residential district of Nishikyo Ward, a roughly 20-minute walk from Hankyu Katsura/Rakusaiguchi. It is the second brand and third shop of the well-loved Kyoto ramen maker Ramen Mugyu, whose flagship sits in the Enmachi (Marutamachi) area. · Described as a brushed-up, new-generation take on classic Kyoto-style back-fat shoyu ramen — refined and approachable rather than extreme, aimed at pleasing both young diners and families. The parent brand sums up its priorities as 自慢のスープ、こだわりの焼き豚 (a soup it is proud of and meticulously made roast pork), and the kitchen wraps up service once the day's chashu runs out. · The signature is a back-fat shoyu ramen: a clear pork stock (豚清湯) generously crowned with chunks of melted back fat, balanced by negi, bean sprouts and chashu, served with medium-thick slightly-wavy wheat noodles from the established maker Teigaku. A wonton-men (ワンタンメン) and a richer 濃厚 bowl round out the lineup, with gyoza, fried rice and karaage as sides.
places.gfd: This is a wheat-noodle ramen shop. The bowls use medium-thick wheat ramen noodles (from producer Teigaku) and a shoyu (soy sauce) tare over a pork broth, plus gyoza, fried rice and karaage on the menu. The dish was born by accident in the 1950s: while working at the original shop, owner Kazuo Yamagishi would eat noodles dipped in broth, zaru-soba style, as a quick staff meal; a regular customer saw it and asked to try the same, and from 1955 it joined the menu as tsukemen. · A defining Kyoto touch: because tsukemen began as a staff meal meant to be eaten fast, the dipping broth was traditionally served only lukewarm, but here it is served piping hot for local tastes. places.chef: owner-couple (husband and wife) · Kyoto, Gion / Yasaka Shinchi · A husband-and-wife team runs this tucked-away Cantonese kitchen in an old Gion building, carrying on the lineage of Hōbu (鳳舞), the legendary Kyoto Chinese restaurant often called the source of "Kyo-chuka" (Kyoto-style Chinese cooking). · Quiet, homey hospitality over flash: a deliberately inconspicuous door, an intimate counter, and an owner who checks in on diners mid-meal so the place feels like eating at someone's home rather than a restaurant. · Karashi soba (カラシソバ) — wheat noodles tossed in mustard and topped with a savory sauce of shrimp, chicken, green onion, bamboo shoot, lettuce, and wood-ear mushroom, built on a chicken stock and Rishiri kombu base, offered in three spice levels playfully named like school grades (中学 middle-school / 高校 high-school / 大学 university).

places.chef: owner · Ramen Okura sits on Ichijoji's famous ramen street in northeast Kyoto, a short walk from Eizan Ichijoji Station. It's a small, no-frills counter shop, the kind of place that runs from lunch deep into the early morning (to 5 a.m.) for students, night workers and ramen-crawlers. · Generous portions and honest value: lunch sets (until 14:00) add just 50 yen to a bowl and come with free rice refills, and the U-shaped counter is built so a solo diner can slip in and eat well without ceremony. · The kitchen lets you pick your broth: shoyu, shio, a punchy garlic bowl, a rich kotteri, and a 'new seafood' (shin-gyokai) ramen built on a stock blended from ten kinds of fish for a clean, collagen-rich umami. places.chef: owner, chef · Kyoto · The owner took up ramen seriously later in life, studying the craft on his own after turning 50, and opened this small shop in a quiet Kitashirakawa residential corner (near Chayama Station on the Eizan line, just south of the famous Ichijoji ramen district) on October 14, 2021. Despite the weathered, old-fashioned lantern signage that makes it look like a decades-old institution, it is a relatively new arrival. · He set out simply to become the neighborhood's beloved ramen shop, building bowls on pure chicken stock with female local chicken and refusing to muddy the soup. Offering a plain kake ramen for just 500 yen is read as quiet confidence in the broth and noodles alone. · Chicken-forward ramen made entirely from poultry stock. The clear shoyu chuka-soba is the chef's calling card, with a clean, transparent broth and medium-straight noodles, while the rich tori-paitan (chicken white broth) is praised as so deep it tastes almost like it contains pork bones. The Half & Half pairs a transparent shoyu seitan broth beneath the creamy chicken paitan in a single bowl that grows richer as you stir.

places.vgd: Every bowl is built on chicken broth (the shop uses female local chicken bones), with pork chashu, and the broth/tare contain animal products throughout. No vegan or vegetarian ramen is offered.

places.chef: owner-chef · Kyoto, Japan · Kinzan opened in 2013 in the quiet Nishioji-Shichijo residential pocket of Shimogyo-ku, a roughly 15-minute walk from JR Nishioji Station. The owner trained at the respected Takabashi Ramen before striking out on his own, and the shop has since grown into a local favorite popular enough to open a second branch near Kyoto City Hall (Shiyakusho-mae). · A Kyoto-rooted approach: classic local-style tonkotsu-shoyu done with carefully chosen regional ingredients (Kyotanba/Kyoto Highland pork from Hiyoshi Farm, Kujo negi, aged soy from the Koyama and Goko breweries, Kondo noodles), cooked in an open kitchen so guests can watch the bowl come together. · The signature bowl is a 'Kyoto black shoyu' (京都黒醤油) ramen: a glossy, near-jet-black soup built on a pork-bone base, given sharpness and depth by aged soy sauce and a mellow sweetness by back fat. It is finished with two styles of Kyoto Highland pork chashu (lean and fatty, torched to order), Kujo green onion, bean sprouts, menma, and a slick of back fat. Straight medium-thin noodles from the long-established Kondo Seimen give a firm, wheaty bite.
places.gfd: Not suitable for celiac/strict gluten-free diners. The ramen is wheat noodles (from Kondo Seimen) in a pork-bone broth seasoned with wheat-based aged soy sauce tare. places.notes: [Mom & Pop] Owner Sakakimoto came to ramen the long way around, spending some fifteen years training in kappo (Japanese fine-dining) and sushi kitchens before striking out on his own. That fine-dining grounding shows in every detail of the bowl.
places.chef: Sakakimoto · owner, chef · This is the second outpost of the Jun chicken-paitan brand, following the original near Marutamachi; it opened in the Shijo-Karasuma area on August 13, 2025. · Owner Sakakimoto came to ramen the long way around, spending some fifteen years training in kappo (Japanese fine-dining) and sushi kitchens before striking out on his own. That fine-dining grounding shows in every detail of the bowl. · Sakakimoto has said that if he was going to open his own place, he wanted to do something only he could do — hence the labor-intensive, single-serving emulsified broth and the kappo-trained attention to finish and presentation. · The signature is a tori-paitan (chicken white-soup) soba in an espuma-like, foamed broth. Rather than ladling from one big pot, the kitchen emulsifies the chicken soup bowl by bowl in a blender, whipping it into a mild, airy, almost cappuccino-like froth. The base is built primarily on Kagoshima chicken, rounded out with small amounts of Miyazaki and Oita pork bones, and paired with custom medium-thick, chewy noodles and rare pork chashu.
places.gfd: This is a chicken-paitan ramen specialist built around custom medium-thick wheat noodles served in a creamy chicken-and-pork-bone broth, with seasoning tare and shoyu/miso variants that typically contain wheat. No gluten-free noodle, dedicated prep, or celiac accommodation is mentioned anywhere. Not safe for celiacs; a strictly gluten-free diner should not eat here.
places.vgd: Every bowl is built on an animal base: a rich chicken (tori-paitan) broth made primarily with Kagoshima chicken, supplemented with Miyazaki and Oita pork bones, and topped with rare pork chashu. places.chef: ramen shop, izakaya offshoot · Kyoto · Toyojiro opened on December 1, 2024 in the Kawaramachi/Kiyamachi area of Kyoto (Yaoyacho, Nakagyo-ku), growing out of the popular tuna-and-wagyu izakaya Toyota (とよ田) and sharing its premises. It represents that team's leap from sake-side beef and tuna plates into a dedicated Jiro-style ramen concept. · To elevate the famously rough, fat-heavy Jiro genre with high-grade wagyu fat rather than ordinary pork back-fat, aiming for a smooth, deep umami that gives ramen fans a more refined take on the style. · A wagyu-forward Jiro-style bowl: a broth built on rendered fat from 48-month-old female cattle from Okazaki Ranch, finished with a soy-sauce or salt tare and crowned with premium wagyu fat. The house signature carries over the izakaya's bokkake (slow-stewed beef tendon) as a topping, giving a bokkake-jiro that fuses wagyu and ramen.
places.gfd: This is conventional Jiro-style ramen: wheat noodles plus a soy-sauce (shoyu) or salt tare, served in an animal-fat broth. Wheat noodles and standard shoyu both contain gluten, and no gluten-free option or gluten-handling practice is mentioned anywhere. Not suitable for celiacs; treat as unsafe.
places.vgd: A Jiro-style ramen shop built around a beef-fat broth (rendered fat from 48-month-old female cattle), wheat noodles, and beef-tendon (bokkake) toppings. There is no vegan or vegetarian bowl here; the entire concept is meat-forward, so a plant-based diner has nothing safe to order.
places.hours: 11:00-22:00, open daily (no regular closed day listed). Note: the ramen offering reportedly runs alongside the evening izakaya operation; lunchtime is recommended for the ramen without a mandatory drink order.

places.chef: owner · Kyoto · Menya Ichiki bills itself as a Kyoto white-miso ramen specialist. It first opened on October 6, 2025 as a tucked-away shop in the Nishijin area, then relocated and reopened on April 22, 2026 in a renovated Kyoto townhouse (machiya) in Shikino Higashino-cho, Kita Ward, along Kitaoji-dori near Kenkun Shrine and Daitoku-ji. · The shop leans into local Kyoto identity — white miso, yuba and fu — to set its bowls apart from typical tonkotsu or shoyu ramen, and keeps a calm, welcoming room where even solo diners are at ease. · The signature bowl is the 京の白味噌らーめん (Kyo no Shiro-miso Ramen): an original tare blending several Kyoto white misos for a gently sweet, creamy soup, married to a bonito-and-kombu dashi. A variation, the 京の白味噌貝だしらーめん, swaps in a shellfish (scallop) dashi for a mellower umami. Bowls come dressed in distinctly Kyoto ingredients — fresh yuba (tofu skin) and fresh fu (wheat gluten) — alongside smoked chashu pork, a soft-boiled egg, white negi and bonito flakes. The chashu is torched just before serving to coax out its aroma and umami. Thick, straight noodles with a firm chew round it out. A rice-and-fried-chicken set can be added.
places.gfd: Not gluten-free. The signature bowl is built on wheat ramen noodles and is topped with fresh fu (生麩, wheat gluten), so there are multiple unavoidable wheat sources in the dish itself. The broth is a white-miso tare with bonito/kombu dashi (miso typically contains wheat or barley as well). No gluten-free menu, dedicated equipment, or celiac accommodation is indicated. A celiac diner cannot eat the ramen here safely.
places.vgd: Not vegan or vegetarian. Both signature bowls are built on animal stock — bonito (katsuobushi)/kombu dashi or a shellfish (kai) dashi — and are topped with smoked chashu pork and a soft-boiled egg. While the yuba (tofu skin) and fresh fu toppings are plant-based, the broth foundation is fish/shellfish-based, so the ramen is not suitable for vegans or vegetarians. No vegan version is advertised.

places.chef: owner-operator · Kumamoto-style ramen · A small ramen counter sitting steps from Kitayama Station and across from the Kyoto Prefectural Botanical Garden, serving the Kumamoto style of tonkotsu in a city better known for lighter Kyoto ramen. The name itself is a wink to its roots: 'mokkosu' is Kumamoto dialect for a stubborn, headstrong, true-to-yourself sort of person. · Diners describe an owner with a meticulous, conscientious touch in the service and presentation, leaning into a robust, full-bodied bowl rather than the lighter Hakata-style tonkotsu. · Kumamoto ramen: a thick, milky-white tonkotsu (pork-bone) broth finished with fragrant burnt-garlic ma-yu oil, served with thin, straight noodles. places.chef: owner · Saiin, Ukyō-ku, Kyoto · Iwamotoya occupies the former 麺匠 一粒万倍 西院店, a branch of a Kyoto ramen group known for lighter chicken-based (Oyama jidori and duck) clear shoyu bowls. places.chef: UNCHI株式会社 (operator) · Osaka, Japan (chain origin) · This is the first Kyoto location of くそオヤジ最後のひとふり, a clam-broth ramen brand under Osaka's UNCHI Co., the company behind the celebrated 'Jinrui Mina Menrui' (人類みな麺類). The original Kuso Oyaji opened in Osaka's Juso district in April 2013, and the brand has since reached overseas markets including New York, China, Korea and Nepal. The Kawaramachi-Sanjo shop opened September 15, 2023, set into the Sanjo shopping arcade with a refined Japanese-style interior — counter seats on the first floor and tables on the second (about 19 seats in all). · The parent company's stated guiding idea is to 'change the world through the power of ramen,' and the broths are made with custom water-purification equipment to draw out a clean shellfish umami meant to be finished to the last drop. · Clam-broth ramen, with the あさりラーメン (asari/short-neck clam ramen, around 980–990 yen) as the signature bowl — a clean clam dashi balanced with a blend of dark and light soy sauce, served with chewy yet firm medium-thick straight noodles and clams as a topping. The shijimi (corbicula) and a limited hamaguri (clam) ramen round out the lineup.
places.gfd: Standard ramen: wheat (medium-thick straight) noodles plus a soy-sauce-based tare (typically wheat-containing). Not celiac-safe and no gluten-free menu is indicated. The broth itself is clam dashi, but the noodles and shoyu tare make the dish unsafe for gluten avoidance.
places.vgd: This is a shellfish-broth ramen specialist — every bowl (asari/shijimi/hamaguri) is built on a clam dashi with soy-sauce tare and contains clams; there are no vegan or vegetarian ramen options.

places.chef: Operated by the team behind the Osaka-area shop 中華そば ふもと (Fumoto) · Osaka (Chuka Soba Fumoto lineage) · Yakimeshi to Men Kyoto opened on April 2, 2025 in the Sanjo-meiten-gai arcade just west of Kawaramachi-Sanjo, as a sister shop from the team behind the well-regarded Osaka-area ramen shop Chuka Soba Fumoto (中華そば 麓/ふもと). places.chef: Miyaji Tamotsu · Cantonese kitchen, tantanmen specialist, family-run · Muko City (Teradocho), Kyoto · Kirin-en opened in 1967, when authentic Cantonese cooking was still a rarity in the then-farmland district of Muko. Founder Miyaji Tamotsu (宮路保) set out to let local residents enjoy genuine Guangdong cuisine casually, and the place has stayed family-run, with Miyaji Ryo (宮路亮) now serving as store manager. · The house motto for its spicy dishes is 「辛くて旨い」— 'spicy but delicious' (うま辛) — chasing flavor and craft rather than heat for its own sake. · A fiery tantanmen built on four kinds of chili plus a house-made meat-miso for depth, which became the restaurant's calling card during Muko City's spicy-food (gekikara) town-revitalization push. In developing it the kitchen reached for the bhut jolokia ('jolokia') pepper — once billed as the world's hottest — and the bowl can be ordered across escalating heat levels (roughly 1 to 5), with the mild steps served without the jolokia powder and the hottest tiers dosed with it.
places.gfd: No gluten-free accommodation found. This is a Cantonese Chinese restaurant whose signature is a chili-laden tantanmen — wheat noodles in a sesame/chili broth, almost certainly built on a wheat-based shoyu/miso tare and a pork base. No allergen or gluten-free information is published on the official site, and nothing indicates celiac-safe handling. A celiac diner should treat this place as not safe.
places.vgd: Not a vegan venue. A traditional Cantonese kitchen with a meat- and seafood-forward menu (the famous tantanmen and black-vinegar sweet-and-sour pork are both meat dishes). No vegan ramen or vegan set is advertised, and tantanmen broth is typically pork/sesame based. A vegan would need to ask, with little likelihood of a fully plant-based bowl.

places.chef: independent local ramen shop · Kyoto (Nishijin / Uzumasa) · A modest, locally beloved ramen shop in the Nishijin district of Kyoto's Kamigyo ward, set along Chiekoin-dori (知恵光院通) near the old textile quarter. It is the second location (2号店) of Ramen Tengu, whose main shop is in Uzumasa in western Kyoto, and it carries a nostalgic Showa-era chuka-soba feel with a hand-painted sign and a cozy room of wrap-around counter and a few low tatami seats. · Keep it simple and let the broth do the work - a clean, comforting Kyoto-style bowl that regulars return for rather than a flashy specialty shop. · The house bowl, Tengu Ramen, is built on a pork-bone broth blended with Japanese-style dashi: it looks rich and is dressed with back-fat, yet drinks surprisingly clean and stays balanced to the last sip. It comes over thin, springy noodles with menma, nori and a chashu so slow-braised it falls apart and melts on the tongue. A generous heap of fresh, crisp scallions is served on the side so you can pile them in to taste, with an extra-scallion (追いネギ) option for about 50 yen.
places.gfd: A wheat-noodle ramen shop. The signature bowl is thin wheat noodles in a pork-bone broth blended with Japanese dashi, almost certainly built on a wheat-based shoyu tare, with chashu and menma. There is no indication of gluten-free noodles, a dedicated preparation area, or allergen handling, and broth/tare are shared. Not suitable for celiacs or strict gluten avoidance.
places.vgd: The base of every bowl is an animal broth (pork bone blended with Japanese dashi), and toppings center on braised pork chashu. No vegetable or vegan broth, no plant-based ramen, and no meatless menu is described. Not a vegan-friendly option.
places.hours: 11:30-22:00 (Tabelog) / some articles list 11:30-23:00. Closed Wednesday (some reports say irregular closures).

When Sugichiyo's original shop was gone, Tengu became the refuge for its devoted fans, carrying
places.chef: owner-chef (former Sugichiyo head cook) · Tokiwa (near Uzumasa), Ukyo-ku, Kyoto · Opened in 2002 by a chef who had headed the kitchen (店長／元料理長) at Sugichiyo (杉千代), a legendary Uzumasa ramen shop that drew lines for its then-revolutionary bowls some two decades ago. When Sugichiyo's original shop was gone, Tengu became the refuge for its devoted fans — described as the sole shop carrying Sugichiyo's DNA forward — and it is the original 2002 shop of the Ramen Kyoto Tengu group. · Carry the Sugichiyo lineage faithfully rather than chase trends: an honest, additive-conscious pork-bone shoyu bowl in a modest storefront, kept welcoming for families, children and women rather than dressed up as a destination shop. · Tengu Ramen (てんぐラーメン): a pork-bone and chicken-gara shoyu broth finished with back fat (背脂) that drinks lighter than it looks, paired with thin low-alkaline straight noodles in the Sugichiyo mold and chashu so tender it falls apart when lifted with chopsticks. A basket of chopped green onion is provided to season the bowl to taste, and rice is famously all-you-can-eat.
places.gfd: Not celiac-safe. This is a classic wheat-noodle ramen shop: the noodles are thin low-alkaline wheat noodles (mirroring the Sugichiyo lineage), the tare is soy-sauce based (shoyu, which in Japan virtually always contains wheat), and gyoza/shumai/shoronpo sides are wheat-wrapped. The pork-bone/chicken broth itself plus heavy shared-pot/shared-fryer use means cross-contamination is unavoidable. No gluten-free menu or noodle substitute is offered.
places.vgd: Not a vegan or vegetarian establishment. The signature bowl is built on a pork-bone (tonkotsu) and chicken-gara broth finished with back fat (背脂), topped with chashu pork. The broth and the standard bowls are animal-based, so there are no genuine vegan or vegetarian ramen options here. A plant-based diner would have no suitable main; ask staff before ordering, but expect no accommodation.
places.hours: Lunch and dinner 11:30-2:00 the next day (L.O. 1:40). No regular closing day.

places.chef: owner, ramen chef · Kyoto (Umezu, Ukyo-ku) · A small ramen specialist tucked into the Umezu neighborhood of Kyoto's Ukyo ward, on the Arashiyama side of the city near the Hankyu Matsuo-taisha line. The shop has been quietly perfecting one thing for over four decades, opening around 1981 and, in the owner's own words, building it up steadily over roughly 45 years in a corner of Kyoto. · The owner's stated aim is simple and warm: once a customer comes in, to earn their return and become a shop they patronize for a lifetime - 'a lifelong asset.' Guests are invited to step in without hesitation and give the ramen a try. · The signature bowl is a Kyoto-style shoyu ramen in the Daiichi-Asahi (第一旭) mold: a pork clear-broth (tonkotsu seitan) made from Miyazaki-raised pork, seasoned with a light soy-sauce tare. Unlike many Kyoto bowls it skips the heavy back-fat float yet still drinks rich, with a generous layer of oil on top - mild in flavor but satisfyingly hearty. It comes crowned with soft, fatty melt-in-the-mouth chashu, thin bean sprouts, and Kujo green onion over thin, low-hydration straight noodles.
places.gfd: This is a traditional Kyoto-style ramen shop. The bowl is built on wheat noodles in a pork-based clear broth seasoned with a light soy-sauce (shoyu) tare, which is wheat-based. Both the noodles and the tare contain wheat/gluten, and there is no gluten-free menu, no separate preparation, and no indication of allergy accommodation. This is not safe for celiacs or those avoiding gluten.
places.vgd: Every bowl is built on a pork bone broth (made from Miyazaki-raised pork) and topped with fatty chashu pork, so the soup itself is animal-based. There are no vegan or vegetarian options on the menu.

places.chef: owner-operated, Chinese-staffed kitchen · Higashiyama, Kyoto · Ryumon is widely regarded as one of Kyoto's pioneers of authentic Sichuan cooking, with its original Higashiyama-Sanjo location anchoring a small family of about four branches across the city. The main shop is run with a genuinely Chinese kitchen and floor — Mandarin is spoken throughout, and the cooking balances heat with depth rather than chasing pure spice. · Honest, homestyle Sichuan food cooked the way it is in China — real Sichuan chilies and peppercorns, big flavors, late into the night — served in an unpretentious neighborhood setting. · The scallion-oil chicken noodles (葱油鶏面, ¥650) are the house signature — an inexpensive bowl that regulars describe as authentic enough to bring a tear to your eye. Alongside them, the fiery Sichuan-peppercorn stir-fried eggplant (¥950) and a properly numbing mapo tofu are the dishes locals come back for.
places.gfd: No gluten-free accommodation indicated. places.chef: 深谷信人 (Fukaya) · owner-chef · Kyoto (Nishikyo-ku, Kashihara) · Rosen is a small, calm house restaurant in the Kashihara neighborhood of Kyoto's Nishikyo Ward, a short walk from Hankyu Katsura Station. Owner-chef Fukaya (深谷信人), a Kameoka native, trained from his teens — culinary school, then the celebrated Sichuan restaurant Kato Hanten (華都飯店) that once sat in Kyoto's Holiday Inn, followed by kitchens in Osaka and Nishinomiya — before going solo to Shanghai to study authentic Chinese cooking. He named the shop after Luzhou (瀘州) in Sichuan and opened in Kashihara about a dozen years ago, and he still hand-makes his doubanjiang, tianmianjiang and douchi and cooks with Kashihara- and Kameoka-grown vegetables. · Authentic Sichuan and Chinese cooking served generously and affordably in an unfussy, settled space — confident portions and honest pricing rather than show, built on house-made seasonings and local produce. · Tantan-men is the house signature, offered in white-sesame and black-sesame versions (with a curry tantan-men alongside). The black-sesame bowl is the standout: a rich, deeply aromatic sesame sauce with gentle sweetness and restrained heat over springy noodles — mellow rat…
places.gfd: No gluten-free provision found. The house specialty is tantan-men, which is wheat noodles in a sesame-rich, meat-based sauce, and the kitchen is a Sichuan/Chinese operation that relies on wheat-based soy sauce and fermented bean paste (doubanjiang). Mapo tofu, yakisoba, and other listed dishes are all gluten-bearing. No dedicated gluten-free menu, no allergen labeling, and no cross-contamination controls were documented anywhere. Treat as not celiac-safe.
places.vgd: Not a vegan or vegetarian-oriented shop. places.chef: Shoichi Iwasaki · owner, head chef · Opened March 2013 in the Nishinokyō neighborhood of Kyoto's Nakagyō Ward, near Nijō Castle and the Sanjō-kai shopping arcade. · Owner-chef Shoichi Iwasaki (岩﨑昭一) spent roughly 15 years training at a celebrated tonkotsu ramen shop in Minoh, Osaka — also his hometown — before opening Yoshiharu on March 11, 2013. After leaving the kitchen where he learned his craft, he spent extensive trial-and-error developing the broth that would become the shop's signature. · Iwasaki aims for a broth that suppresses the heavy off-odor often associated with pork bone, delivering deep umami and richness with a clean, light finish — a balance of 'umami, richness, and depth.' The shop frames its mission as making ramen — broth, noodles and chashu — that cannot be replicated elsewhere. · A 'Minoh-style' tonkotsu — distinct from Kyushu tonkotsu — built on a creamy white broth of pork skull and knuckle bones, chicken carcass and chicken feet (momiji), finished with quality back fat, pork skin and plenty of vegetables, then simmered for 24+ hours. The flagship bowl is the special tonkotsu ramen with straight thin noodles, soft sweet chashu, green onion and bean sprouts…
places.gfd: Not gluten-free safe. This is a classic wheat-noodle ramen shop — straight thin wheat noodles in a pork-bone broth, with gyoza (wheat skins) and fried rice/karaage on the menu. A celiac diner should not eat the ramen here.
places.vgd: Not vegan-friendly. The entire identity of the shop is a pork-bone (plus chicken carcass and chicken-feet) broth simmered 24+ hours, topped with chashu pork. places.chef: female owner · Kyoto — a new concept from the three-generation Motomachi Ramen family, set in a renovated traditional wooden machiya on Ninenzaka. · ichiren is a newer yuzu-ramen specialist tucked into an alley just off Ninenzaka, a couple of minutes' walk below Kiyomizu-dera and Kodai-ji, opened May 16, 2021. It is a fresh brand launched by the family behind Motomachi Ramen (元町ラーメン), a Kyoto ramen name carried across three generations, so the bowls draw on a long local lineage while being reworked into something refined and contemporary. · To carry forward Kyoto tradition while evolving it into a refined, distinctly Kyoto ramen — built around yuzu and a calm white-and-yuzu-toned interior meant to be welcoming for solo diners and especially women. · Yuzu-forward Kyoto ramen. The namesake 一蓮 (Ichiren) is a rich double broth of pork bone and chicken bones brightened with yuzu; 紗 (Sara) is a clearer fish-dashi bowl (grilled flying fish, bonito, mackerel, sardine) also scented with yuzu; and the 豆乳柚子 (soy milk yuzu) bowl is creamy yet light. Bowls come with tsukune, and tables offer tororo kombu, yuzu-shichimi and yuzu-kosho to shift the flavor mid-meal.
places.gfd: No gluten-free provision. This is a wheat-noodle ramen shop: the signature bowls use thin/thick wheat noodles in pork-and-chicken or fish-dashi broths, and standard ramen tare contains wheat-based soy sauce. No dedicated gluten-free menu, no allergen statement, and no celiac-safe handling is published. Not safe for celiacs; even the soy milk yuzu bowl is served over wheat noodles.
places.vgd: Not a vegan shop. The two core bowls are pork-bone/chicken broth (一蓮) and fish-dashi broth (紗), each topped with tsukune (meatball) and chashu/egg. places.chef: owner-operator · Kyoto · Opened February 7, 2026 in the Nishi-Kamogamo / Omiya-Yakushiyama corner of Kita-ku, taking over a space that had previously housed another ramen shop. It is a small independent counter built around one idea: a Kyoto bowl you could eat every single day. · "毎日食べられるラーメン" — ramen you can eat every day. The seasoning is kept gentle on purpose, the chashu is cooked soft so it appeals across all ages, and the noodles are made in-house: medium-thick angular straight noodles at 25% hydration, rested a day, with egg white worked in to push the wheat aroma that Kyoto diners favor. · The house pork-shoyu ramen. The broth is a pork clear-soup (豚清湯) made from only pork arm meat and back fat — deliberately no pork bone — so it lands light yet rich ("あっさりコクうま"), then seasoned with Goko (五光), a traditional Kyoto soy sauce, for that familiar nostalgic Kyoto sharpness. The signature move is chashu, piled without restraint: the standard Buta-yado Ramen (¥950) carries 150g, and the Buta-yado Chashu-men (¥1,200) goes to a 210g mountain of tender, thinly-sliced pork arm. A lighter Buta-yasumi Ramen (¥700) keeps just 30g for a quieter bowl.
places.gfd: Not gluten-free. The bowls are built on house-made wheat noodles (中太の角ストレート麺 with egg white added for a wheat aroma), seasoned with Kyoto Goko soy sauce tare, which is wheat-based. places.vgd: Not vegan. The entire concept is pork-centric: the broth is made solely from animal ingredients (豚ウデ肉・背脂 — pork arm meat and back fat), and the shop's identity is generous chashu (sliced pork). The soy-sauce tare and side dishes are pork-based as well. There is no vegetable broth or plant-based bowl.

places.chef: Saifullah · owner · Kyoto · Ayam-YA grew out of a ramen company whose very first shop opened not in Japan but in Seattle. When the team brought the concept home to Japan's hyper-competitive ramen scene, they struggled to draw crowds, until an Indonesian exchange student asked a simple question that changed everything: 'Do you use only chicken?' That was the moment the founders learned that many visitors could not eat ordinary ramen for religious reasons. Determined to let Muslim travelers in Kyoto enjoy a real bowl of Japanese ramen with peace of mind, they reformulated the recipe and pursued halal certification through the Malaysia Halal Corporation. 'Ayam' means 'chicken' in Indonesian and Malay. · Make a genuinely delicious Japanese ramen that observant Muslims and curious travelers alike can eat with peace of mind, by keeping the kitchen free of pork and alcohol and building flavor honestly from chicken rather than additives. · Tori-paitan (rich chicken) ramen served as the basic shoyu (soy) chicken soba and a richer shio (salt) chicken bowl, with miso also offered; the broths lean on chicken with a seafood aroma for depth, finished with finely minced onion and scallion, and m…

No gluten-free noodle or gluten-free preparation is advertised, so it is not suitable for celiac diners. Halal does not mean gluten-free.
places.vgd: The house style is tori-paitan (rich chicken broth) and the signature bowls are chicken-based, so the standard menu is not vegan or vegetarian. The kitchen is halal (no pork, no alcohol) and avoids chemical seasonings, which makes it ingredient-conscious, but a plant-based diner would need to ask directly whether anything meat-free can be prepared and should not assume a vegan option exists.
