places.chef: machi-chuka diner, local lunch and dinner spot · Nishikyogoku, Kyoto · A neighborhood machi-chuka (Japanese-style Chinese) restaurant that has fed the Nishikyogoku district for roughly 40 years, just east of Hankyu Nishikyogoku Station on Hanayacho-dori. It draws a cross-section of locals, from solo diners on their lunch break to families, in a bright, big-windowed room with a warm, unpretentious feel. · Honest, generous, affordable home-style Chinese cooking for the neighborhood — big portions, courteous service, and prices that keep regulars coming back day after day. · The signature bowl is the maabo-tenshinhan (mapo Tianjin rice): a fluffy egg over rice blanketed in a generous, glossy mapo sauce. The sauce is built on house-made fermented black bean paste (豆鼓醤) and several chili pastes with ginger and plenty of garlic, given depth by coarsely minced salted fermented black beans (豆鼓の粒) and finished with house chili oil, with finely minced pork for richness — kept addictively savory rather than punishingly hot, served around 1,050 yen with soup and pickles.
places.gfd: No gluten-free provision. This is a Japanese-style Chinese diner built on wheat: noodles, gyoza wrappers, and sauces thickened/seasoned with wheat-based soy sauce and likely doubanjiang. The signature mapo Tianjin rice rides on a mapo sauce that almost certainly contains wheat soy seasoning. There is no indication of gluten-free menus, dedicated equipment, or allergen handling. Not suitable for celiacs.
places.vgd: No vegan offering. The kitchen is meat- and seafood-forward: pork features in the mapo sauce, gyoza, fried chicken, and broths; dishes use animal-based stocks. Even otherwise plant-leaning items (fried rice, ankake) are cooked with meat/egg and shared woks. No vegetarian or vegan menu is advertised.
places.hours: Mon, Tue, Thu-Sun & holidays: 11:00-14:00 and 17:00-21:00 (lunch open also listed as 11:30 on some sources). Closed Wednesdays. Open during holidays, Golden Week and Obon. Some sources note occasional irregular closures.

places.notes: [Mom & Pop] A small, refined Sichuan-leaning Chinese kitchen tucked into a quiet stretch of Nijo-dori just south of the Imperial Palace, opened in 2013 and run single-handedly by its chef-owner. He came up through the produce markets before cooking, and that background shows in his sourcing
places.chef: owner, chef · Kyoto (Nakagyo-ku, Gosho-minami / Karasuma-Oike area) · A small, refined Sichuan-leaning Chinese kitchen tucked into a quiet stretch of Nijo-dori just south of the Imperial Palace, opened in 2013 and run single-handedly by its chef-owner. He came up through the produce markets before cooking, and that background shows in his sourcing — a cook with a reliable eye for ingredients who keeps the menu deliberately compact. · Keep the cooking simple and let quality ingredients carry it — the kind of place where, as one chef put it, everything you order somehow tastes good. Heat is balanced and aromatic rather than punishing. · Sichuan-style cooking pitched a notch upscale rather than fiery for its own sake: a fragrant tantanmen (the lunchtime dry 汁なし version is especially praised), a mapo tofu where the Sichuan pepper and chili oil are rounded out by the sweetness of the ground pork, plus boiled dumplings and sweet-and-sour pork.
places.gfd: A Sichuan Chinese kitchen built around wheat. The tantanmen and dumpling skins are wheat-flour, the chili/sesame tare and seasonings used in dishes like the mapo tofu lean on soy-based and bean-paste condiments that typically contain wheat, and there is no gluten-free menu or protocol. Not suitable for celiacs. A coeliac diner could ask whether any single rice- or vegetable-based plate could be prepared plainly, but cross-contact in a one-cook wok kitchen is unavoidable — treat as not GF-safe.
places.vgd: Not a vegan specialist. The signature bowls (tantanmen, mapo tofu, boiled dumplings, sweet-and-sour pork) all use pork and/or animal-derived broth and condiments. There is no marked vegan option. Because it is a small a-la-carte Sichuan kitchen run by one chef, a vegan might be able to ask in advance for a plain vegetable stir-fry, but nothing is confirmed plant-based, so reserve and ask directly…
places.hours: Dinner 18:00-21:00 (L.O. ~20:30). Lunch not currently served (as of recent listing). Closed Sunday; Monday occasionally closed (~twice monthly); irregular temporary closures possible.

places.chef: owner · 大阪（人類みな麺類系列） · Ramen Daisenso ("Ramen World War") is the Kyoto outpost of the acclaimed Osaka ramen group behind Jinrui Mina Menrui, the much-queued shop that turned shoyu ramen into something theatrical. This branch opened in October 2022 on the first floor of a renovated Kawaramachi building (formerly a sushi restaurant) and marked the group's first move into Kyoto. · A noodle-first house: the noodle-making room is visible from the street, signalling pride in house-made noodles, paired with generous service — diners can add up to five chashu slices and get a free half-portion noodle refill (kaedama). · The flagship bowl is the Kansai-dashi shoyu ramen named 'Pistol' (ピストル) — a clear, light-bodied shoyu broth built on Nagoya Cochin chicken bones and scallop, with deep umami and a faint natural sweetness. The lineup of four soy-based bowls also includes 'Heiwa' (平和), 'Sabita Katana' (錆びた刀, a brothless/soupless shoyu), and 'Jiyu' (自由).
places.gfd: A wheat-noodle ramen specialist whose signature bowls are built on soy-sauce (shoyu) tare, which in Japan is almost always brewed with wheat. Both the noodles and the seasoning base contain gluten, and no gluten-free menu or noodle option is indicated. Not suitable for celiac diners.
places.vgd: All four signature bowls are animal-based: the broths are made from chicken bones (Nagoya Cochin), scallop, and fish/dashi elements, and chashu (pork) is a centerpiece. No vegan or vegetarian ramen is offered.
places.hours: 11:00-00:00 (L.O. 23:30), open daily. (Some local listings note 11:00-22:30; the official store information on the listing shows until midnight.)

It has been described as a味 (taste) protected for roughly four decades by the family runnin
places.chef: old-established independent late-night ramen counter · 博多長浜ラーメン みよし opened in 1983 (昭和58年) in Kyoto's Kiyamachi/Sanjo entertainment district and has become an old-school local institution — '京都の人間でその名を知らぬ者はいない' (there is no one in Kyoto who doesn't know its name). For roughly four decades it has carried the same Hakata Nagahama taste, its small open counter running late into the night. · A purist, no-frills tonkotsu shop: keep the pork-bone broth going, add nothing unnecessary, and let each diner build their own flavor with the tabletop condiments. Regulars even treat certain moves (like adding pepper or curry powder) as 'forbidden,' and finishing by pouring extra broth over rice is part of the ritual. · Essentially one bowl done one way: Hakata Nagahama-style tonkotsu ramen — a clean, gently sweet pork-bone broth paired with ultra-thin Hakata straight noodles. Diners customize at the table with around eleven free toppings (beni-shoga pickled ginger, coarse ichimi chili, tenkasu tempura scraps, sesame, etc.) and can order kaedama noodle refills, which is treated as part of doing Nagahama ramen 'your way.'
places.gfd: This is a Hakata-style tonkotsu ramen shop built around wheat noodles (ultra-thin Hakata straight noodles) in a pork-bone broth, with kaedama (noodle refills) as a core part of the experience. There are no gluten-free noodle or broth options, and no dedicated gluten-free preparation. Not suitable for celiac diners. No allergen handling information was found.
places.vgd: The entire concept is a long-simmered pork-bone (tonkotsu) broth — the shop's identity is its pork broth, kept going continuously. There is essentially one ramen, animal-based, with toppings like chashu (pork). No vegan or even vegetarian bowl is offered.

places.chef: ramen shop, late-night eatery · 四条大宮商店街 / 壬生, central Kyoto · A late-night neighborhood ramen counter sitting right inside the Shijo-Omiya shopping arcade, a few steps from Hankyu Omiya Station. It runs from late morning straight through to around 2 AM, shifting from a lunchtime rush, to evening drinkers ordering sides with beer, to a sudden surge of customers chasing the last trains. · The whole shop is built around one idea — 毎日でも食べられるラーメン, 'ramen you could eat every day' — leaning on accessible, balanced flavor rather than heavy gimmickry, using selected ingredients like Kyoto Tanba highland pork and Kujo negi. · Their core bowl is a classic Kyoto-style se-abura shoyu (back-fat soy-sauce) tonkotsu ramen: a pork-bone broth finished with back fat over thin, easy-slurping noodles, topped with chashu, with branch menus extending to shoyu-pork, chashu-men, and a miso ramen made with miso shipped from Hokkaido.

There is no indication of any gluten-free noodle, tare, or menu item, no dedicated equipment, and shared pots/cooking surfaces make cross-contamination unavoidable. Not suitable for celiac diners.
places.vgd: The entire concept is a pork-bone (tonkotsu) and back-fat broth with pork chashu and toppings such as a boiled egg; sides include karaage and gyoza. There is no vegan or even vegetarian ramen on offer and no plant-based broth alternative noted. Not suitable for vegans.

places.vgd: No vegan options. Broth is pork-bone based; ramen is topped with sliced pork. No plant-based ramen or sides are offered.

places.chef: Independently operated local Chinese restaurant / 町中華, Part of the small 龍門 group in Kyoto · Kyoto (Sichuan-style Chinese cooking). · 龍門 is a small Kyoto chain of authentic Sichuan / neighborhood-Chinese (町中華) restaurants run by 株式会社長城, with the Honten near Sanjo-Higashioji and branches in Okazaki and here in Uzumasa, in Ukyo-ku near the Arashiyama (Randen) line and JR Uzumasa. places.vgd: A meat-and-seafood-forward Chinese kitchen — the house specialty centers on fried chicken and chicken oil, and stocks/sauces are animal-based. places.chef: independent ramen shop, second location of Ramen Mugyu · Tucked into a narrow alley just off Takoyakushi-dori near Karasuma, Ramen Mugyu Vol.2 is the second outpost of the original Ramen Mugyu, whose Vol.1 shop is in the Enmachi (円町) area. The shop occupies a converted townhouse-style space with a long counter and a relaxed, almost izakaya-like feel; guests are handed paper aprons on arrival to keep the splatter off. · The kitchen leans into a clean, sharp Kyoto-style shoyu profile — proper soy richness with a subtle seafood undertone and a clear chicken backbone — that diners have compared to the old-school Kyoto tradition of Shinpuku Saikan. · The signature bowl is the "Onibara Kuro" (鬼腹黒) shoyu ramen: a soy-forward broth built on purebred Nagoya Cochin chicken (純系名古屋コーチン) and aged dried bonito (本枯れ節), brightened with a re-steeped premium soy sauce from Ehime's Kajita shoyu, and finished with medium-thin straight noodles and a fan of extremely thin-sliced pork belly chashu that blankets the bowl. A lighter "Onibara Shiro" (白, white) version and a rich chicken soba (濃厚鶏そば / nōkō torisoba) round out the lineup.
places.gfd: This is a classic wheat-noodle ramen shop. The bowls use medium-thin straight wheat noodles in a soy (shoyu) tare broth, so both the noodles and the seasoning base contain wheat/gluten. No gluten-free noodles or menu are mentioned anywhere. Not suitable for celiac diners.
places.vgd: The signature bowls are built on a chicken (Nagoya Cochin) and dried-bonito broth and are topped with thin-sliced pork belly chashu. The soup is animal-based and there is no vegan or vegetarian ramen on the menu.

places.chef: Kirameki Group (キラメキノ未来株式会社) operator · Kyoto, Japan · キラメキノ青空 is a Kyoto-grown ramen and mazesoba brand run by the Kirameki Group (キラメキノ未来株式会社), known across Kansai as one of the pioneers of Taiwan-style mazesoba. The group operates a spread of shops through Kyoto — in student and downtown neighborhoods such as Yamanouchi (山ノ内) and Tanaka near Kyoto University — and out into Osaka, Shiga and Nara as part of a stated '30-store project'; this Shijo-Muromachi shop (下京区鶏鉾町), a short walk from Shijo-Karasuma, opened as one of its newer locations. · The shop leans into bold, concentrated flavor and customization: diners are encouraged to tune their bowl with a lemon wedge and the tabletop condiments to shift the heavy chicken broth across the meal. · A thick, intensely rich tori-paitan (chicken white broth) ramen, offered in both a 'shio no Kirameki' salt version and a shoyu version, built on chicken paitan with niboshi and topped with chashu, menma and green onion, with a lemon wedge for mid-bowl 味変. The kitchen also turns out Taiwan mazesoba and a newer dan-dan mazesoba.
places.gfd: This is a standard ramen and mazesoba shop. The bowls are built on wheat ramen noodles, with a wheat-based shoyu/tare element and a rich chicken broth, so they are not suitable for celiac or strict gluten-free diners. There is no gluten-free menu, no gluten-free noodle option, and no indication of any allergen-handling or dedicated preparation. Even the "shio" (salt) version of the chicken paitan is served over wheat noodles. Treat this as not gluten-free.
places.vgd: The house style is built around a thick chicken (tori-paitan) broth, with chicken chashu and other meat toppings; the Taiwan mazesoba and dan-dan dishes use minced meat. There is no vegan or vegetarian ramen on offer and no plant-based broth alternative. Not suitable for vegans or vegetarians.

places.chef: owner · Kyoto · A Katsura-neighborhood outpost of the long-running Kyoto ramen name Daiichi Asahi, this shop carries on a recipe and reputation built over more than fifty years, passed down through the noren-wake tradition of opening a branch under the founding house's name and methods. · Despite the richness of the pork-and-soy foundation, the broth leans on plenty of simmered vegetable stock to finish clean and light on the palate, the balance Daiichi Asahi is known for. places.gfd: This is a classic Kyoto-style chuka-soba shop: the ramen is built on wheat noodles in a pork-bone-and-soy-sauce (shoyu) broth, and the soy-sauce tare is almost certainly wheat-based. places.vgd: The house broth is a pork-bone (tonkotsu) base finished with soy sauce, and signature bowls are topped with chashu/roast pork. There is no vegan or vegetarian ramen offering noted; even a plain bowl would carry the pork broth. Not suitable for vegans.

places.chef: owner · Fushimi, Kyoto · A long-loved neighborhood Chinese kitchen (町中華) standing at the northwest corner of Oote-dori and Kyomachi-dori, right in front of Fushimi-Momoyama Station and a minute from Momoyama-Goryomae. It has become a fixture for locals who come for serious cooking served in an unfussy, drop-in setting, with a wood-floored dining room and an adjacent same-name café for Western dishes and coffee. · No flashiness, just reliable depth — whatever you order is dependably good, and the heat is kept mild enough that even spice-averse diners can enjoy the tantanmen. · Sesame-forward tantanmen and, in the cold months, the house's signature sake-lees ramen and sake-lees tantanmen — a nod to Fushimi's sake-brewing heritage. The sake-lees ramen dissolves sake lees into a clear (清湯) chicken-, pork- and vegetable-based soup, finished with char siu and vegetables; the sake-lees tantanmen layers the lees over a rich house-sesame paste and house chili oil, topped with sweet-miso minced pork.
places.gfd: Not gluten-free safe. The ramen and tantanmen are built on wheat noodles, and the broths use a soy-sauce (wheat shoyu) and sesame base over chicken/pork/vegetable stock; the sake-lees ramen dissolves sake lees into a soy-ramen base and is topped with char siu. places.chef: owner · 京都市中京区壬生馬場町（壬生エリア） · 麺屋 栩羚廚（くれいず）opened on September 12, 2024 on Kouin-dori between Shijo-Omiya and Sanjo-Senbon, an area of central Kyoto in the middle of a wave of new ramen openings. It is a small, design-conscious counter shop that put down roots fast: within months it had drawn a steady following and, in February 2025, opened a second branch in Tokyo's Nakameguro. · A 'material-commitment' approach paired with careful plating — a richly concentrated pork broth that locals rate among the thickest in Kyoto yet keeps the typical tonkotsu off-smell in check, served with attentive hospitality in a stylish little room. · The house specialty is an extremely thick, creamy Kyoto-pork tonkotsu. Two core styles anchor the menu — a 濃厚豚骨醤油 (rich tonkotsu-shoyu) and the 極濃豚骨, a paste-thick 'doro-kei' broth poured with a layer of flavorful tare on top that you stir in before eating; a 旨辛豚骨 spiced with ichimi togarashi sits between them. The signature bowl is the limited 極濃豚骨味玉 (¥1,250), built on flat, chewy wheat noodles from the respected Teigaku (棣鄂) noodle maker and finished with squared-cut chashu, a marinated egg, bamboo shoots, and scallion.
places.gfd: No gluten-free options. The bowls are built on wheat noodles (from the Teigaku/棣鄂 noodle maker), a tonkotsu broth finished with what is almost certainly a wheat-based shoyu tare, and a flour-dredged karaage side. There is no indication of any gluten-free preparation or separate handling, so this is not suitable for celiac diners.
places.vgd: Not vegan-friendly. The entire concept is an ultra-rich pork-bone (tonkotsu) broth, with chashu, marinated egg, and other animal toppings; even the side dishes are meat. No plant-based broth or noodle option is offered.

places.vgd: Not vegan or vegetarian friendly. places.chef: owner-operator · Ono, Yamashina-ku, Kyoto · Iwasaki Tanmen opened its doors on March 1, 2023 in the Ono neighborhood of Yamashina, just steps from Ono Station, taking over a storefront that previously housed another ramen shop (Shioemon). It is a rarity in Kyoto: a shop devoted to tanmen, a vegetable-piled salt ramen far more common in the Kanto region of eastern Japan than here in Kansai. · Make-it-your-own simplicity: diners can dial the vegetables, pork, noodle quantity, garlic and spice to taste, and garlic is served on the side so each guest controls their own portion. Sides like gyoza, karaage and takana rice round out an honest, affordable bowl. · The house tanmen is the signature: a mound of lightly stir-fried vegetables — cabbage, bean sprouts and more — over medium straight noodles in a chicken-and-pork salt (shio) broth. It arrives looking hearty and Jiro-esque, yet the soup is surprisingly clean and light, with no heavy back-fat. A pot of house chili-miso (kara-miso) sits at hand so you can stir in heat and depth gradually as you eat.
places.gfd: Not gluten-free friendly. Tanmen is built on wheat ramen noodles in a salt (shio) tare; the broth and house salt sauce are not documented as wheat-free, and there are no gluten-free noodle or accommodation options on the menu. No allergen handling is documented. Anyone with celiac disease or wheat allergy should treat this as unsafe.
places.vgd: Not suitable for vegans or vegetarians. The signature tanmen is a chicken-bone and pork-based salt broth topped with stir-fried pork and vegetables; pork and a chicken/pork stock are integral to every bowl. No plant-based broth or vegetable-only version is documented. A diner could potentially ask about a vegetable-heavy customization, but the base soup is animal-derived.

places.chef: Inoue (proprietor) · owner, chef · Ichijoji, Sakyo-ku, Kyoto — on the city's famous Ichijoji ramen street, but a deliberate step away from the heavy-broth pack. · The shop is the latest evolution of a Kyoto noodle maker who has spent years chasing dashi rather than richness. The lineage runs from a dashi-based ramen shop, Isao (イサオ, opened 2010), which the owner renamed and reframed in 2014 as Odashi to Komugi 130 (おだしと小麦 一三〇) to put the dashi and the wheat front and center. In June 2022 the concept was distilled again into だし料理 十. · The whole place is built so customers can actually understand dashi — you can watch it being made, taste it, and talk it through with the owner. Seasoning is pared back to almost nothing so the stock itself carries the bowl. · The signature bowl is the breakfast-only o-dashi no new-men: a clear soup built from just three things — Rishiri kombu, sawara (young Spanish mackerel / sagoshi), and bonito flakes — seasoned with a single gram of Iwate salt and no soy sauce at all. No dedicated gluten-free preparation is advertised; a celiac diner would need to ask directly and likely cannot be accommodated.
places.vgd: Not vegan or vegetarian. The dashi is entirely animal-based (sawara/Spanish mackerel, bonito flakes, plus kombu), and the noodles contain egg. There is no plant-based bowl on offer.

places.chef: owner, founder · Kyoto (Kitayama district yatai origins); founder from Kanazawa · Kyoto Kitayama Motomachi Ramen traces its roots to a street cart (yatai) that the first-generation owner — a native of Kanazawa — set up on Shinmachi-dori in Kyoto's Kitayama district roughly 50 years ago. Drawing on the rich, dark soy-sauce style of nearby Toyama Black, he built a Kyoto take on the bowl using tamari soy sauce from a long-established local soy-sauce maker. The business later moved into a permanent shop, settling at its current location in an alley off Higashinotoin in central Kyoto, where the cart's original flavor is carried on by a later (third) generation. · Honor the original yatai flavor while continuing to refine it; serve until the broth is gone and then close for the day. · A rich black-soy-sauce ramen finished with plenty of back fat (背脂醤油らーめん), with beef-tendon ramen (牛すじらーめん) as a second signature. The defining element is a specialty tamari soy sauce of the kind used for eel sauce, sourced from a 160-year-old Kyoto soy-sauce maker.

places.vgd: No vegan or vegetarian options. The broth is a rich black soy sauce ramen built on pork/beef bases (beef tendon is a signature), the noodles are wheat, and the tare uses wheat-containing tamari soy sauce. Nothing on the menu is plant-based.

One course a month of about ten dishes: seafood from Mie ama divers, A5 wagyu, and two or three clay-pot rices at the end (one regular keeps lunch light on Tagawa days). Spring brings a flower-pepper hot pot, autumn a Matsutake feast. Tabelog Award Bronze every year from 2018 to 2026; the shop's site says it holds a Michelin star. One course for everyone at once, about a dozen plates with two pasta courses, light and playful rather than heavy: an 11-vegetable tart, panzerotti of porcini and lobster, a dan-dan-inspired pistachio capellini. Pairings come from a walk-in cellar of some 600 bottles. Tabelog Award Bronze 2019, 2025 and 2026, Italian WEST 100 (2021, 2023, 2025), and a Michelin Guide Kyoto Osaka 2026 Selected restaurant. places.notes: [French · Tomikoji-Nijo, a former Chinese-cuisine chef's French in a kimono merchant's house] A Taisho-era kimono merchant's house of about 100 years on Tomikoji-dori, renovated into a high-ceilinged dining room looking onto a courtyard garden. Chef Motoi Maeda, born in Kyoto in 1976, spent about ten years cooking Chinese food at a Kyoto hotel, then trained in Burgundy and at Pittoresque and HAJIME before opening here in 2012. The cooking is French with Chinese accents: a cold mapo tofu of tofu mousse, wagyu meat-miso and chili oil is the dish everyone mentions, alongside a salad of some 50 Ohara vegetables and condiments such as fermented black beans and dried shrimp. The chef forages watercress on the Kamo River and hunts game in Niigata. Courses change each visit, and the shop asks about previous visits when you book. Tabelog Award Bronze every year from 2019 to 2026. 2026 diners loved the room and the surprises; a few found the service thin. Closed Wednesdays and Thursdays.

places.notes: [Meat kaiseki · Gion, a self-taught owner's all-wagyu counter] A two-storey wooden house a step off Hanamikoji, reached down a narrow path between textured earthen walls, with eight seats at a hinoki counter (renovated in 2023). Owner Tsutomu Ito came to meat through a friend who graded beef and a first taste of beef butchered that same day, is self-taught as a cook, and opened in the owner's home town of Gion at the end of 2004 under the family name Miyoshi; the building had been the owner's mother's salon. One course a month runs through a dozen beef dishes — tongue cured on kombu, beef sashimi, shabu-shabu, steak and sukiyaki — between seasonal seafood and vegetables, and ends with rice and egg yolk. Tabelog Award 2026 Silver; a 2026 reviewer notes a Michelin star from 2018 to 2022. Upstairs is a one-group inn where diners can eat and then sleep. places.notes: [Kappo · Higashiyama, a forager's "museum of food" opposite Shoren-in] Across the lane from the gate of Shoren-in, behind a plaque reading Shun Gyuan and a tea-house approach, eight seats face a tatami-topped counter, an okudo stove and shelves of antique jars. Owner Masanori Tsukioka, from Hokkaido, began cooking at 15 in Sapporo, trained around Japan including under Hisao Nakahigashi at Kusakui Nakahigashi, ran Jimi Kougetsu in Kusatsu, and moved to the United States in 2019 to open a restaurant, but COVID ended the plan and the chef restarted in Kyoto, opening here in 2021. The chef buys at markets and fishing ports and serves the day's best with wit and some theatre: abalone porridge, a cutlassfish so big it is called a dragon, sushi handed across the counter, a dessert of corn tempura. Born in Nara in 1961 into a family of cooks, the chef ran Fujita in Pontocho at 27 and opened Gion Sasaki in 1998, moving here in 2006; 2026 reviewers note seven straight years of three Michelin stars. One July 2026 diner found the apprentices did most of the cooking that day. Book by phone at the start of each month for two months ahead. Lunch ¥22,000, dinner ¥44,000 all in.

Chef Wataru Hayashi, more than fifty years in the trade, has run the place for over thirty: plain, deeply seasoned Kyoto cooking without show, from a shrimp dumpling soup to a salt-grilled sea bream collar and a cold rice porridge. There is no menu and no explanation — the house style is to let you guess. The counter is hushed (one diner found it tense) and allows no photos; the upstairs rooms are more relaxed. Lunch from about ¥15,700 is the gentle way in. Tabelog Silver or Bronze every year since 2019. Closed Wednesdays; JCB and AMEX only.

Chef Kentaro Nishibuchi, from Joyo in Kyoto Prefecture, learned Chinese cooking for six years at Kakan in the Kyoto Brighton Hotel, then five years of Japanese cooking at Gion Sasaki, and opened here in 2013. The result is gentle, layered Chinese food: shark fin braised and then grilled in superior broth, chicken wings stuffed with bird's nest, fried rice lightened with grated daikon. Diners in 2026 praise the chef's warm smile and call it very hard to book. Tabelog Silver every year since 2019. Cash only; closed Sundays.

The founder, from 門前仲町 in Tokyo, opened in 1948 and created the oxtail stew that still simmers in a big pot behind the counter, its sauce topped up for over 77 years; the second generation turned it into meat kappo. There is no menu: the staff lead you from cold oxtail soup through beef-tongue, heart and tripe sashimi to grilled cuts and the stew, which you finish by picking up the bones. The counter cannot be booked, so queue before 18:00. Now run by fourth-generation Yoshifumi Sakakibara with family. Tabelog Bronze 2025–2026. Closed Sundays and holidays.

places.notes: [Sweets · Rokkaku-dori, the monthly Kohaku Nagashi] Behind a confectioner's shopfront in a late-Edo townhouse — the house dates from 1885 and is credited with bringing castella to Kyoto — a quiet tea room looks onto a small garden. People come for the Kohaku Nagashi: trembling, glass-clear agar under a syrup that changes each month, grape in September, chestnut zenzai in October, persimmon in November. The warabi mochi is so soft it barely holds on the chopsticks. Write your name on the list when it is full; holiday waits run about half an hour. Around ¥1,000; cards accepted; closed Wednesdays.

places.notes: [Sweets · Kyoto Station, an azuki tea room inside the Shinkansen gates] The station outlet of Housendo, the Shimogamo bean specialist whose owner travels to Tanba every year for the best black soybeans and dainagon azuki. Staff check whether you are in a hurry for your train. It is inside the Shinkansen gates, so only for travellers holding a Shinkansen ticket. Zenzai about ¥1,400; open daily.

Monthly kaiseki is cooked with deep-well "Yasaka water", the grilled course finished in front of you. Unusually, a fully plant-based course can be arranged, and maiko can be booked to entertain. Lunch from ¥12,100, kaiseki ¥36,300; book by the day before. Reviewers in 2026 range from rapt to lukewarm on value.

Ten seats at a single-slab counter face a small garden; two private rooms are upstairs. Sixth-generation 中村元計 (Motokazu Nakamura) — once a Zen trainee at 天龍寺 and now a doctor of food science — keeps the two dishes passed from father to son: sake-grilled guji, finished as a soup with hot water over the bones, and a white-miso zoni made without dashi. Courses are served in quiet private rooms over a courtyard; reviewers note three Michelin stars. Lunch around ¥20,000–30,000, dinner ¥40,000–50,000; book ahead; closed Sundays.
places.chef: Motokazu Nakamura (中村元計; official site, sixth-generation master, with the romaji Motokazu Nakamura) · Sixth-generation master (official site) · Per the official site: founded in Bunsei 10 (1827) when the first master, 若狭屋清兵衛, carried Wakasa fish such as guji and mackerel to Kyoto for the palace and court nobles; the second generation began catering; the third, a tea devotee, made tea kaiseki catering the core; the fourth supplied the inns 柊家, 俵屋 and 炭家 during the war; after the war the restaurant opened on its present site, and the fifth generation built today's base. The sixth, 中村元計, studied at Tokyo University of Fisheries, trained as a Zen monk at 天龍寺 in 嵯峨嵐山, and in 2021 earned a doctorate in food and agricultural science at 龍谷大学, approaching cooking as science. Tabelog Award Bronze 2017–2023; Japanese cuisine WEST "Tabelog 100" 2021. 2026 reviews call it Michelin three-starred. · 「即味心也」 — taste is the heart: only a person's heart moves another's (official site). · Sake-grilled guji; white-miso zoni.

Matcha is whisked to order and served with a monaka. A good stop after Shimogamo Shrine or Kibune. Around ¥1,000–1,600; cards and QR payments accepted; closed Tuesdays.

Eat it the same day. Cash only; closed Wednesday and Thursday.

Small bags from ¥750 make light, long-keeping gifts. Takeaway only; come early; closed Wednesdays.

places.notes: [French · Gion, a Ducasse alumnus on Kyoto's south side] Chef Yosuke Yamaji — Hotel Okura, the Institut Paul Bocuse in Lyon, then Alain Ducasse au Plaza Athénée in Paris — cooks creative French with Kyoto seasons and produce from the family farm, in an eighteen-seat room with a counter, four tables and a small courtyard. Sommelier-manager Maeda leads warm service, and the team sees guests off at the door. Lunch from ¥6,800 is a good-value entry; dinner from ¥12,000. 2026 opinions vary: most praise the sauces and presentation, a few found it salty or slow. Closed Wednesdays.

places.notes: [Pizza · Karasuma-Oike, the neighbourhood Neapolitan] A plain, office-like front on Anekoji-dori hides a lively pizzeria where pizzaioli work a wood-fired oven behind a high counter. The crust is the star — crisp at the edge, chewy within, good to the last bite even cold — under classics like Margherita and funghi with Parmigiano grated at the table, or a fiery house salami. Spoon on the spicy basil oil. Antipasti like ham with tuna sauce are worth extra bread. Pizzas ¥1,900–2,500; lunch is easier than dinner. Closed Thursdays.

The mixed sandwich and the firm, caramel-topped pudding are just as loved, and the coffee is rich and balanced; beans are sold to take home. Upstairs, a western-style lunch room keeps shorter hours. Pancake set ¥1,400; weekday afternoons have the shortest waits. Open daily 8:00–19:00; AMEX only.

places.cu: Retro kissaten that carries on two closed Kyoto shops: the coffee house Kissa Seven (the building) and the western-style restaurant Corona (its egg sandwich) (official site) · Corona egg sandwich: a thick, hot dashi omelette on bread spread with demi-glace and mustard, ¥1,180 · Set A breakfast with two pieces of it, salad, prosciutto, soup, yogurt and a drink ¥1,800 (November 2026) · thick toast,…
places.notes: [Kissaten · Karasuma Oike, the Corona egg sandwich] A retro coffee house in a building that was Kissa Seven for about 50 years from 1963; after its master died in 2011, the son looked for someone to keep the shop going, and Madrague opened that September. About a year later the free paper 音読 asked the shop to carry on the famous egg sandwich of Corona, a western-style restaurant that had just closed, and Corona's master came to teach it in person. The result is a fist-sized, hot, dashi-soft omelette on bread with demi-glace and mustard (¥1,180) — cut it in half to eat. Breakfast sets until 11:00; book a seat for 8:00, 9:30 or 12:00. Open daily 8:00–18:00 (irregular closures); cash only.
places.chef: Owner (unnamed on the official site), who opened the shop with the owner’s wife · Per the official site: before opening, the owner managed a café tied to the revival of Kyoto townhouses and old shopping streets and wanted to get back to hands-on work; while looking for a property with the owner’s wife, the couple met the son of the master of Kissa Seven (in business from 1963 for about 50 years; the master died in 2011) and opened Kissa Madrague there in September 2011. The name is that of Brigitte Bardot’s villa in Saint-Tropez; the owner’s wife loved the actress. The owner once worked part-time at Francois, near Corona, and often ate Corona’s egg sandwich on breaks. The site also describes a team, 京都喫茶文化遺産, formed to take over and keep old neighbourhood kissaten. Tabelog Kissaten "Tabelog 100" 2021, 2022, 2026. · Per the official site: to keep "the long-running neighbourhood kissaten with tradition", not a retro-styled café, and hand it on to the next generation. · Corona egg sandwich; Set A breakfast.

The line forms from 16:30 and the owner hangs the noren at 17:00. Almost every table orders the duck roast; the shime saba, kumiage yuba and Kyoto-style oden (the octopus takes time — order it early) are the other classics. The menu shows no prices, yet bills run around ¥4,000–6,000. Book a table for 17:00 or 19:00; the 11 counter seats are first come. Cash only; smoking allowed; closed Sunday.

Order kuzumochi (¥1,200), the shop's kuzukiri with black syrup, or the seasonal jo-namagashi — chestnut kinton in autumn — with sencha, or come early for the fruit sandwiches, which can be gone before noon. Take a number at the machine; no bookings. One October 2026 visitor found the prices high for Gion and was asked to pay 30 minutes before closing. 11:00–18:00, closed Monday.

Not fast, but the water is refilled and you are seen off warmly. No reservations; 11:30–14:00 and 16:30–23:00, closed Monday.

places.notes: [Tai-meshi · Kawaramachi, Uwajima's sea bream rice by the Takase River] A townhouse restaurant down a back street on the Takase River, past a small inner garden, where a couple from Uwajima in Ehime serve their home town's tai-meshi: thin slices of raw sea bream in the house dashi soy sauce, eaten first as sashimi, then over rice, then with an egg yolk on top. Lunch gozen from ¥2,200 (double sea bream ¥2,860), served until the fish runs out; the mikan juice is pressed from the okami's brother's Uwajima orchard. Courses (¥6,600 lunch, ¥16,500 dinner) need booking two days ahead. One August 2026 reviewer found the taste simple, like a basic egg over rice.

places.notes: [Kappo · Kiyamachi, Shinji Tokuo's counter] A Kiyamachi kappo by the Takase River, open since 2005, where Shinji Tokuo buys at the market each morning and cooks without show: "food you never tire of", in the shop's words. Sit at the polished zelkova counter for omakase courses — lunch ¥10,800, dinner ¥24,000, tax and service included — of sashimi, soft-shelled turtle chawanmushi, wasabi wagyu steak, homemade karasumi with daikon and Saikyo-miso fish; marunabe turtle hot pot is the house dish. Reviewers praise the warm welcome from the chef, the proprietress and the young staff. Tabelog Bronze 2017–2021. Lunch Wed–Sat, dinner Tue–Sat; book lunch a day ahead. One April 2026 reviewer wrote that the shop generally does not take bookings from inbound tourists.
places.chef: Shinji Tokuo (徳尾真次) · Owner-chef · Kyoto Prefecture (official staff page) · Per the official site: 日本料理とくを marked its 21st anniversary on 11 February 2026; the staff page lists 徳尾 真次 (born 19 January, from Kyoto Prefecture, hobbies travel and playing in a band) and four more staff, from Fukuoka and Amami Ōshima (Kagoshima); "私も含め、スタッフも若い者ばかりです" (the owner and the staff are all young). Tabelog’s shop text names the chef as Shinji Tokuo and says the owner goes to the market every morning. An April 2026 regular describes the head chef as "sometimes a band member, sometimes a horse owner, and sometimes a loving traveler", says the shop has been run with the proprietress for over 20 years, and that it serves black soybeans and young Tsukahara bamboo shoots year after year. Tabelog Award Bronze 2017–2021; Tabelog Japanese cuisine WEST "Tabelog 100" 2021. · Per the official site: dishes that make the most of the ingredients bought every day, handled lightly — no showy effects, but food you never tire of; Japanese cuisine to be enjoyed more casually. · Marunabe (soft-shelled turtle hot pot); charcoal-grilled wagyu; karasumi daikon.

places.notes: [Yakitori · Shijo Omiya, a one-cook charcoal counter] An eight-seat yakitori counter in a quiet street near Shijo-Omiya, opened in 2023 by Kato, who cooked at Kyoto's Torisaki before: skewers of Date chicken grilled over strong, direct charcoal heat in the Torishiki manner, eleven to a course with pickles, chicken soup, a rice bowl and dessert. ¥17,000 covers the food and all the drinks (¥15,000 with soft drinks). Kato grills and serves alone, and reviewers single out the warmth of the welcome; one July 2026 regular calls the gizzard "undoubtedly the best I've ever had". Two seatings, 17:00 and 20:30; reservations only, hard to get — watch Instagram for cancellations. Tabelog Yakitori WEST 100 2024, 2025.
places.chef: Kato · Owner-chef, who grills and serves alone (2026 reviews: "The owner, Mr. Kato") · Per 2026 reviews: Kato previously worked at Torisaki in Kyoto (February, May and September 2026), and the shop grills in the Torishiki style (February and May 2026). A July 2026 reviewer writes that only two places in Kyoto handle Date chicken — the master’s restaurant and Tori Kago, run by one of the master’s apprentices — and that the meat is soaked in baking-soda water to loosen it from the bone and the shiitake sun-dried for half a day. places.notes: [Café · Kawaramachi, a two-floor townhouse café down an alley] Through a narrow entrance in the Kayukoji alley, a few steps from Kawaramachi Stn, the room opens into a surprisingly large old wooden house with heavy beams, retro counter seats downstairs, roomy table seating upstairs, and rows of manga on display. Lunch is generous plates at about ¥1,280–1,350 (kara-age, curry, taco rice), afternoons are coffee and house cakes, and at night it turns to drinks and small plates until 22:00. A line forms at noon, so phone ahead; seating is 90 minutes. Part of SARASA, a Kyoto café company dating from 1984; this shop opened in 2007. Cash only; closed Wednesday.

places.notes: [Strawberry sweets · Karasuma Oike, a strawberry-only patisserie] A small white-and-brown shop off Sanjo where every cake is a strawberry cake. Founder Mika Watabe was working in fashion design when a friend brought round some remarkably good strawberries; the visit to the grower behind them led to the first shop in 2003. Fully ripe berries now come straight from farms around Japan, a different variety each day. The premium shortcake (about ¥1,450–1,595) layers strawberries inside and on top; the mille-feuille comes tied with a ribbon you snip with tiny scissors. Nine café seats, no bookings; 11:00–17:00 every day. Prices are high, as reviewers note.
places.chef: Mika Watabe (渡部美佳) · Founder (official site profile: Mika Watabe), Representative director of 株式会社ミュウ, the operating company (official company page: 代表取締役 渡部美佳) · Lives in Kyoto City (official site). · Per the official site: while working in fashion planning and design, Watabe was so moved by strawberries a friend introduced that the shop for strawberry sweets opened in 2003; the farm that grew those berries became a contract grower, sending only berries ripened in the field. The site credits Watabe with more than 100 recipes across Japanese, Western and Chinese sweets, appearances on TV, in magazines and at events, and work as an adviser on strawberry breeding for agricultural research bodies. Company history: opened in April 2003 on Senbon-dori in Kamigyo-ku; moved to Sanjo, Nakagyo-ku, in March 2014 (Tabelog: 9 March 2014); the company was set up in March 2013, has a strawberry laboratory and production atelier in Okayama Prefecture, and lists 株式会社三越伊勢丹, 株式会社大丸松坂屋百貨店, 株式会社高島屋 and 株式会社阪急阪神百貨店 as trading partners. places.notes: [Bar · Gion Shinbashi, a hidden machiya cocktail bar] Off a stone-paved Gion lane by the Shirakawa, a dark gate you might not take for an entrance leads down a lit stone path to a century-old townhouse: tatami private rooms along the corridor, then a high-ceilinged room with a one-slab counter facing a glowing back bar and an illuminated garden. Seasonal fresh-fruit cocktails and well-made classics (Martini, Rob Roy), plenty of single malt, and non-alcoholic or lighter drinks on request. Cover ¥1,100; two drinks with cover ¥4,700 in May 2026. Open nightly 18:00–02:00. A sister bar of Gion's FINLANDIA BAR.

places.notes: [Vegetable-led restaurant · Shijo Kawaramachi, a greenhouse room four floors up] The restaurant of GOOD NATURE STATION, next to Takashimaya: a room full of plants with an open-atrium terrace, cooking mostly Kyoto-grown vegetables simply. Lunch is a seasonal set with a medicinal-food theme — five small deli dishes, soup, a main of Tanba chicken or Kyoto pork, multigrain rice and a small dessert (¥2,500–3,400 in 2026); dinner turns to wine with caprese, duck-ragù pasta, venison and Kameoka beef. Terrace seats carry a table charge, and a September 2026 diner on the open terrace worried about the many birds overhead. Book online; 11:30–16:00 and 17:30–22:00.
places.chef: Hotel restaurant; no chef or manager is named in the sources · Opened 9 December 2019 (Tabelog) on the 4th floor of GOOD NATURE STATION, the building of GOOD NATURE HOTEL KYOTO (official site; 2026 reviews). A July 2026 reviewer describes it as part of the Keihan group. Lunch sets change with the seasons; a repeat diner who visited from 2022 to October 2026 described the winter set as a way to experience "Winter Nourishment" through food and the lunch sets as medicinal-herb sets, and a July 2022 visit found an afternoon-tea wellness set themed on "Yaku Shoku Dougen" (the synergy of medicine and food). · Per Tabelog (the restaurant’s own text): ingredients, mainly vegetables, are sourced from local producers in Kyoto and cooked simply to bring out their character; the lunch course pairs "sauces that embody the essence of French cuisine" with Kyoto and Japanese flavours. · Seasonal vegetable lunch sets; Kameoka beef and venison at dinner.
places.gfd: Ask, and tell the restaurant in advance: it asks guests with allergies to say so beforehand and warns that, depending on the allergy, it may not be able to adapt on the day (Tabelog). places.notes: [Tarte tatin café · Okazaki, half a century of tarte tatin] A small, old-fashioned café near Heian Shrine devoted to tarte tatin. Its story starts with the café 紅屋 that Yuri Matsunaga and husband 辰夫 opened in Gion in 1959; it became an art gallery, moved here in 1971 as a French restaurant beside the gallery, and turned into this café in 1987. Yuri kept baking the tarte tatin — honoured in France by the Confrérie des Lichonneux de tarte tatin in 2006 — until dying in 2014, and a grandchild bakes it now. About 20 apples go into each tart; pick from the day's varieties (Fuji ¥950 in 2026) and eat it warm with yogurt. No bookings; Tuesday–Sunday 11:30–18:00.
places.chef: Maya Wakabayashi · Granddaughter of the founder, named in a January 2016 article as carrying on the recipe; the official site says the recipe is now baked by the founder’s grandchild · Per the official site: the first owners, 松永ユリ (Yuri Matsunaga in Leaf Kyoto and Fashion Headline) and 辰夫, opened the café 紅屋, forerunner of LA VOITURE, in Gion in 1959; out of a love of art it became the gallery 紅 in 1964; in 1971 the business moved to Okazaki, where the French restaurant LA VOITURE opened alongside the gallery. Yuri, captivated by the tarte tatin served as a French dessert, kept baking it and was admitted in France to the Confrérie des Lichonneux de tarte tatin in 2006. The official site gives Yuri’s death in 2014 at 96; a January 2016 Fashion Headline article says Yuri died "two years ago at the age of 92", was born in the Taisho era, always sat in a corner of the shop, and created the recipe after eating tarte tatin on a trip to France. Leaf Kyoto (March 2021) adds that the daughter, Tomomi, helped open the 1971 restaurant and that the shop became a tarte tatin café in 1987. The maker on the online shop is the company 株式会社 紅 at the shop address. Tabelog Sweets WEST "Tabelog 100" …

The tempura udon — big shrimp, a fluffy egg-thickened broth — and the dashi curry udon are what most reviewers order; any bowl can be had with soba instead. places.notes: [French · Marutamachi, six seats and three ingredients a plate] A six-seat French restaurant on a quiet street near Jingu-Marutamachi, opened in 2012, with wood and stone like a chef's home and dishes on Kiyomizu-ware made with the artists. Only an omakase course: ingredients picked from producers, gently cooked at low temperature, no more than three on a plate — the egg 'Homage to the Master' with maple syrup, a tomato consommé drunk from a matcha bowl, venison with foie-gras-stuffed Manganji pepper. Lunch ¥11,000, dinner ¥22,000 (+10%). Book by phone two days ahead (overseas guests via Pocket Concierge); smart casual. Closed Wednesday and the second and third Thursday.
places.chef: Akai · Chef ("Chef Akai" in a February 2026 review); sommelier-qualified (official site) · Opened 26 November 2012 (Tabelog). Per the operator’s Tabelog text: 13 consecutive years in the Michelin Guide and 7 in Gault & Millau; Tabelog French WEST "Tabelog 100" 2021, 2023, 2025. Per the official site: the chef visits producers, buys directly, and works with ceramic artists on one-of-a-kind dishes; suppliers named in 2026 news include 桃里庵 peaches from Okayama, asparagus from ジェットファーム長谷川 and あいち鴨 duck from Toyohashi; in October 2026 the restaurant held its first curry event at じんぐうみち, an event space by Heian Shrine. · Per the official site: "素材 × 火入れ × シンプル" — share the vegetables and ingredients producers have raised with care, cook them with the heat the chef has in mind, and finish them as simply as possible with a sense of the season. Per the Michelin Guide: no more than three ingredients on a plate, so a diner can tell what is on the plate. · Omakase course; 師へのオマージュ egg; tomato consommé.
places.gfd: Ask when booking. A single omakase course with bread (ciabatta, baguette), pastry desserts and butter or wine sauces; the shop asks guests to state allergies and disliked ingredients in advance and cannot change the menu on the day (Tabelog; 2025–26 reviews).
places.vgd: Not vegan: the omakase course is built on fish, shellfish, meat, foie gras, consommé and egg, and the menu is not changed on the day (Tabelog; 2025–26 reviews).
places.hours: Lunch 11:30 (last entry 12:00); dinner 18:00 (last entry 19:00); Tabelog gives 11:30–15:00 and 18:00–23:00. Closed Wednesday and the second and third Thursday (may vary); summer break 16–22 August 2026 (official site; Tabelog). Reservation only, by phone, at least two days ahead (same day sometimes…

places.notes: [Izakaya · Kawaramachi, natural wine behind a red door] A small two-floor bistro-izakaya with a red front and benches outside, a short alley off Kawaramachi, open from midday: natural wines chosen to your taste, and plates cooked by one chef who studied natural wine and French cuisine — flap steak, dashi omelette, raisin butter, beet salads, mussels, a chestnut soup in autumn. Portions are big and scaled to the group; order at least two drinks each; the menu has no prices, and reviewers paid about ¥2,000–10,000 a head. Japanese menu only — the shop asks you to try ordering in Japanese. Hours change day to day; check the site or Instagram.
places.chef: Chef (unnamed), who cooks almost everything alone (official site) · Per the official site (in English): "We’re an izakaya, not a bar"; the chef studied natural wine and French cuisine; one chef makes almost everything. The site lists a sister shop 200 m away, chichi (croissant soft-serve, wine and a gallery space), and sells ekaki goods (stickers, plates, glasses, a logo long-tee). Opened 20 May 2015 (Tabelog). An April 2026 reviewer heard that the owner is sometimes in and sometimes not, which can change the menu; on the second visit the beef steak was not available. · Per the official site: "let’s enjoy good food, good drinks, and a good time together!" · Beef flap steak; dashi omelette; raisin butter.
places.gfd: Ask. The menu mixes fritters, fries, spring-roll sausages, quiche, gratin, toast and pasta with salads, cheeses, charcuterie and grilled meat; no gluten information (official menu).
places.vgd: Ask. A few vegetable plates (salted boiled peanuts, black edamame pickles, salads, fritters, fries with black shichimi) sit among meat, cheese and egg dishes; dishes are cooked to the size of the group, so ask (official menu; March 2026).
places.hours: 12:00–22:00 daily (Tabelog), but hours vary: the official site posts the day’s hours (4 November: 15:00–22:00, for drinkers only), and a reviewer advises checking Instagram (April 2026). places.notes: [Izakaya · Shinkyogoku, a 1927 tavern with an abacus at the till] A real Showa-era taishu sakaba on the Shinkyogoku arcade, opened in 1927 by a founder who had come from Asakusa after the Great Kanto Earthquake, as a 'ten-sen shokudo' where everything cost ten sen. The marble counter and tables are the originals. Drink from noon at the counter or share a long table: Kirin draft, Gekkeikan sake, homemade croquettes (¥800), kizushi, oden, aji fry. A red slip goes to the register, where the bill is added on an abacus. Cash only; smoking allowed; at least one drink and one dish each. Closed Tuesday. One long-time customer found the food rushed and a server loud in October 2026, but keeps coming for the building and the atmosphere.
places.chef: Owner at the register (unnamed in the sources) · Per the official site: the first owner moved from Asakusa in Tokyo after the Great Kanto Earthquake and opened the shop in 1927 (Showa 2) in a Taisho-era building, as a "ten-sen shokudo" where everything cost ten sen; at first there was also a Stand north shop, and stalls in Yasaka Shrine and Maruyama Park in cherry-blossom season; the marble counter and tables are as they were at the founding, along with an early electric register and early-Showa posters. The site calls it "real Showa retro", not made up. Reviews in 2026 describe the owner at the register adding bills on a five-bead abacus. · Per the official site: the menu keeps the taste, recipes and work of the founder’s day. · Homemade croquette; oden; set meals.
places.gfd: Not gluten-free in practice: much of the menu is breaded and fried (croquettes, tonkatsu, mixed fry, aji fry, eel tempura), with ramen, fried noodles, curries and shumai (official menu; 2026 reviews).

places.notes: [Yakiniku · Bukkoji-Aburanokoji, a family's lean-beef counter] A small, retro neighbourhood yakiniku house run by a family, where the owner steers you through four cuts in a set order — ichibo steak, yaki-shabu, premium tongue, then filet — each with its own sauce; one regular's group added the premium tripe and tetchan and found them a pleasant surprise. A September 2026 bill for a group of plates came to ¥13,600; most reviewers paid ¥6,000–10,000 a head. In Tabelog's Yakiniku or Grill 100 lists in 2018 and every year from 2020 to 2026. Cash only; book well ahead; 17:00–21:30, closed Wednesday.
places.chef: Family-run (unnamed in the sources) · Per reviews: "run by a family" in blue work aprons (August 2025); a regular wrote in September 2026 that "the usual mother wasn’t there, and it was just the father and son running the place"; the owner recommends the cuts and the order (2026 reviews), and a hostess explains which sauce goes with which cut (July 2026). places.notes: [Creative izakaya · Kiyomizu-Gojo, eight seats behind green tiles] An eight-seat counter down an alley near Kiyomizu-Gojo, behind deep-green tiled walls, open from 15:00: genre-free small plates that reviewers come back for — wagyu-cheek dote-ni skewers (¥900), rare-fried seasonal fish katsu with chive sauce, croquette potato salad, burrata spring rolls, water eggplant with homemade karasumi — with wines picked to your taste. Two staff look after the counter. ¥1,000 a head covers the appetiser and service; most bills are ¥10,000–15,000. Book on TableCheck weeks ahead; closed 2–3 days a week (see Instagram). Tabelog Izakaya WEST 100 2026.

An August 2026 reviewer calls it a restaurant recommended by "Michelin-starred Matsui". Tabelog Izakaya WEST "Tabelog 100" 2026. · Wagyu-cheek dote-ni skewers; rare fish katsu with chive sauce; croquette potato salad.

places.notes: [Curry · Shinkyogoku, European-style curry in a stone-paved alley] A small curry shop on the quiet, stone-paved Yanagikoji, a few steps from the Shinkyogoku arcade, where the smell of curry carries into the alley. The curry is European-style — gently spiced, a little sweet — with the sauce served apart from saffron rice dressed with vegetables, on pretty tableware. Lunch Set A (¥1,500 with salad, pickles and coffee, September 2026) and the fuller Course A with soup and caramel banana pudding are the usual orders; seasonal curries change through the year. One diner first visited about 35 years ago. Curry only (no tea-and-cake orders), no photos, cash only; closed Tuesday.
places.chef: Owner (unnamed in the sources) · A May 2025 reviewer had first visited about 35 years earlier and noted that the interior had since been updated. · European-style curry with saffron rice; caramel banana pudding.

places.notes: [Curry · Kawaramachi, Kyoto-style soup curry in clay pots] A small second-floor soup curry shop behind Kawaramachi OPA that gives the Hokkaido dish a Kyoto turn: a dashi-tasting broth with more than 15 spices, Kyoto Akajidori chicken and the Kyoto beef brand 京の肉, and a pile of fried vegetables, served piping hot in an orange clay pot. The chicken drumstick soup curry (¥1,580) is the house pick; there is a vegetable soup curry too (¥1,280, dashi base). Spice runs in 7 levels, but reviewers found even level 5 mild (June 2026). Lunch queues are common — book a 11:30 or 17:30 slot through Instagram. One-hour seating; cards accepted.
places.chef: Owner (unnamed on the official site, which calls the chicken drumstick curry 店主オススメ) · Per the official site: formerly named 土鍋スープカレー近江屋清右衛門; a sister shop of the European-style curry shop CLAY POT CURRY OHMIYA; the shop studied which chicken suits its soup curry and settled on Kyoto Akajidori; vegetables come direct from contract farms around Japan; the clay pots are handmade Mashiko ware. Tabelog gives the opening as 21 August 2018. · Kyoto Akajidori chicken drumstick soup curry; beef braised in red wine.
places.gfd: Ask. Soup curry on a Japanese dashi base with fried vegetables, rice and toppings such as cheese and fried onion; no gluten information (official site; 2026 reviews).

places.cu: The Nishiki shop of an old Kyoto nama-fu (fresh wheat gluten) maker that supplies ryotei (official site) · fu manju: house-made smooth bean paste in aonori-flavoured nama-fu, wrapped in a bamboo leaf, ¥330 (August 2026) or ¥350 (September 2026) · fu taiyaki, small and baked to order, ¥352 (October 2026) · summer shaved ice Sasa no Tsu with bean paste ¥400 (August 2026) · nama-fu to cook at home ·…
places.notes: [Wagashi · Nishiki Market, fu manju from an old nama-fu maker] The Nishiki Market counter of Fuka, a nama-fu maker that has supplied fresh wheat gluten to the Imperial Palace and to Kyoto ryotei since at least the 1860s. The thing to get is the fu manju its own history says Fuka created: smooth bean paste wrapped in chewy, aonori-green fu and a bamboo leaf (¥330–350), eaten chilled. Small fu taiyaki are baked to order (¥352). Two seats and a counter for eating on the spot, with Ippodo bancha for ¥100. 10:00–17:30, closed Monday.
places.chef: Owner, the 7th generation (official site; unnamed) · Per the official site: Fuka has long supplied fu to the Kyoto Imperial Palace; its founding year is unknown because its records burned in the upheavals of the late Edo period, but a pass for entering the palace is dated in the Keio era (1865–68), and the present owner is the 7th generation counted from then. Fuka helped bring nama-fu from plain temple cooking into Kyoto cuisine by delivering it fresh to ryotei every morning, and still works mainly to order for ryotei, making 30–40 kinds a day by hand from pumped groundwater with about 20 craftsmen, all of whom study the tea ceremony. The site says Fuka made the first nama-fu manju, an idea attributed to Emperor Meiji, who liked nama-fu. Tabelog Wagashi WEST "Tabelog 100" 2023 and 2026. · Per the official site: the family business is "craft, not commerce" — use natural ingredients as far as possible and make by hand everything it can. · Fu manju; fu taiyaki.
places.gfd: Not gluten-free: nama-fu is wheat gluten mixed with glutinous rice flour and steamed, and the fu manju and fu taiyaki are made from it (official site; 2026 reviews).
places.vgd: The fu manju is described as house-made smooth bean paste wrapped in nama-fu (wheat gluten and glutinous rice flour) flavoured with aonori and rolled in a bamboo leaf, with no animal ingredient named; a full ingredient list was not seen, so check (official site).
places.hours: 10:00–17:30; closed Monday, and on the last Sunday of each month from February to August (Tabelog; the official site gives 10:00–17:30, closed Monday). places.notes: [Wagashi · Gion, an old yokan shop down an alley] A small, Showa-feeling yokan shop hidden in an alley just off Shijo-dori in Gion, founded in 1884 according to reviewers. There is no one at the counter: ring the bell and the owner comes out (one reviewer describes a man in a white chef’s coat and black cap). The famous chestnut steamed yokan, packed with chunks of chestnut and wrapped in bamboo leaf (¥2,000), is seasonal — in September 2026 some visitors bought it and others were told it was not yet being made; there is also a silky mizu yokan, and small chilled steamed yokan (¥350) to eat on a walk. Flavours sell out by late afternoon — phone ahead for the big ones. Several reviewers call the service brusque. Cash only; closed Sunday.
places.chef: Owner (unnamed in the sources) · September 2026 reviews give the founding as 1884 (Meiji 17), and one calls it the first shop in Kyoto to make mizu yokan. Tabelog Sweets "Tabelog 100" 2017 and Sweets WEST 2018–2020, 2022; Wagashi WEST 2023 and 2026. · Chestnut steamed yokan; mizu yokan.
places.gfd: Ask. A September 2026 buyer read the mizu yokan label as only adzuki beans, sugar and agar, but the steamed yokan (mushi yokan) ingredients were not reported and the shop publishes none; ask before buying (2026 reviews).
places.vgd: The mizu yokan label lists only adzuki beans, sugar and agar (a September 2026 review); the steamed yokan in chestnut, hojicha, kinako and matcha flavours have no ingredient list in the sources (2026 reviews).

places.notes: [Pâtisserie café · Kawaramachi, canelés and parfaits on a back street] A 10-seat café on the quiet street behind Kawaramachi OPA, run by the owner of the French restaurant Le cadeau. It began with baked goods — the canelé is the thing to take away — and now makes tall seasonal parfaits (strawberry in spring, figs in autumn, ¥2,500 with a drink), cakes crowned with a butterfly tuile, and lunch plates of pie or quiche with plenty of vegetables (under ¥1,500 with a drink in 2026). You may get to watch your parfait being made. 12:00–19:00, closed Thursday; check Instagram for extra closures.
places.chef: Owner, who runs the French restaurant Le cadeau (unnamed in the sources read) · Per rurubu (September 2024): the owner runs the French restaurant Le cadeau, which serves a late-night dessert course to one booked party at a time; Au point de rendez-vous started by selling baked goods and now serves parfaits and lunch; the 2024 açaí bowl was overseen by the Le cadeau chef. A December 2022 reviewer says the shop opened in May 2022 and that its Christmas dessert course was supervised by "Chef Imoto", with pastry chef Kaede and staff member Kokoro each devising a plate; a July 2024 reviewer quotes the shop calling itself the "sister store of a Michelin-listed establishment". A 2025 reviewer mentions a "Canelé Day" on the 21st of each month and occasional cooking classes. · Canelés; seasonal parfaits; butterfly-tuile cakes.

places.notes: [Trattoria · Kawaramachi, pizza and pasta until midnight] A 40-seat second-floor trattoria a couple of minutes from Kawaramachi Station, done in bright blue walls and sofas, open 18:00 to midnight. Thin, crisp pizza from a 500 °C oven, the house spaghetti with chili and sansho, a mixed antipasto plate and a steak with mustard are what reviewers order; Friday is wine day at ¥700 a glass. Built for groups: free-flow courses from ¥5,000 and private hire for up to 50. One drink per person; smoking allowed. Closed Thursday.

Per the shop’s own Tabelog text: seasonal Kyoto ingredients, authentic crisp pizza and a signature chili-and-sansho spaghetti at reasonable prices; banquets, after-parties and weddings for up to 40 guests. · Per Tabelog (the shop’s own text): an adult hideaway offering "the perfect satisfaction that’s neither too cheap nor too expensive." · Pizza; chili-and-sansho spaghetti.
places.gfd: Ask. Pizza and spaghetti (Barilla No. 3) are the core; steak, salads, carpaccio and ajillo are also on the menu, but no gluten information is published (Tabelog; 2024–26 reviews).

A ¥1,000 starter charge brings small dishes such as shijimi soup. Most 2026 reviewers spent ¥8,000–15,000 a head. Book ahead; tables may be limited to two hours. Closed Tuesday and Wednesday.

places.notes: [Curry · Shijo Karasuma, one keema, very spicy] A 14-seat curry counter in the Muromachi back streets that serves a single dish: keema curry, beef and pork or chicken, stir-fried to order with a 17-spice mix, topped with grilled vegetables and an umeboshi, with homemade pickles and optional onion achaar. Tabelog Curry WEST "Tabelog 100" 2019, 2020, 2023, 2024, 2026. · Keema curry (beef and pork, or chicken).

places.notes: [Sushi · Shijo-Kawaramachi, old-style counter] A family sushi counter up the first lane off Kawaramachi north of Shijo, in business for over 50 years: a U-shaped counter of 17 seats, large cuts on traditional rice, and the house negima soup of tuna and leek. A long-time regular found in January 2023 that the previous owner had handed over to a son. Omakase of 8 pieces was ¥2,640 in 2023; a set was ¥3,300 before tax in January 2025, and 8 thick slices of chu-toro sashimi ¥3,300 in February 2026. One dish per person; cash only. 17:00–22:00, closed Thursday; book by phone.

places.notes: [Bar · Shinkyogoku, a drink from 3 pm] A standing bar with a small terrace at the mouth of the Hanayu Koji alley off Shinkyogoku, opened in 2013 by K-stage, the company that runs Gion's Finlandia Bar; it was named for the aurora, as a curtain of light over the alley. No cover charge and most drinks in the low ¥1,000s: gin and tonics with Earl Grey or yuzu (¥1,300), seasonal fruit Bellinis, a long whisky list. A year-end regular praises the young manager's knowledge; smoking is allowed inside, so non-smokers take the terrace. 15:00–23:00.
places.chef: Bar of K-stage (株式会社ケイ・ステージ), which also runs ぎをん FINLANDIA BAR, The Common One Bar Kyoto, Turquoise Bar and ぎをん新橋 何生庵 · Per the K-stage company history: in August 2013 the company opened The Northern Lights Corner on the ground floor and the more formal Bar The Northern Lights on the first floor of the new Hare no Hi Hanayu Koji building in Shinkyogoku (the upstairs bar closed in December 2021; the space is now an office of アルコ・ノルディック株式会社, the company’s vodka importer). places.notes: [Italian · Yasaka Pagoda, Kyoto as an Italian region] Chef-owner Yasuhiro Sasajima's restaurant in a converted townhouse right beside the Yasaka Pagoda, open since 2002 and built on one idea: what if Italy had a region called Kyoto? Courses only, lunch from ¥6,000 and dinner from ¥12,000 (plus tax and service): Kyoto vegetables and seasonal fish, two pastas with cheese or truffle grated at the table, charcoal-grilled meat. Italian WEST Tabelog 100 (2021, 2023, 2025). One September 2026 diner found the floor short-staffed. Lunch and dinner, closed Tuesday and Wednesday; book online.
places.chef: Yasuhiro Sasajima (笹島保弘) · Owner-chef (オーナーシェフ, official site) · Osaka Prefecture (Serai, 2013) · Born in Osaka Prefecture in 1964 (Serai, from its spring 2013 issue). Bunshun Online (2017) recalls the chef at イル・パッパラルド in Kyoto, with generous, energetic, reasonably priced plates, and dates the chef’s independence to 2002, launching IL GHIOTTONE as "Italian sent out from Kyoto": courses based on kombu dashi, scented with kinome and yuzu, with Kyoto vegetables such as Kujo leek and Shogoin turnip. Serai gives the Kyoto opening as 2002 and a Marunouchi (Tokyo) branch as 2005; the official site now lists the Kyoto honten, the wine shop Officina IL GHIOTTONE KYOTO (which also sells the group’s frozen pasta sauces) and IL GHIOTTONE DI PIÙ in Grand Front Osaka. Tabelog Italian WEST "Tabelog 100" 2021, 2023 and 2025. places.notes: [Beef-offal kappo · Yanagi-koji off Shijo] A small two-storey house on the stone-paved Yanagi-koji alley, named after the nearby Hachibei Myojin shrine, serving beef offal as Kyoto-style kappo. Lunch is a harami rice bowl with vegetables (¥2,500), no booking. Closed Tuesday.
places.chef: Owner-chef (unnamed in the sources); run by the yagenbori group · Per the yagenbori group site: one of the group’s six Kyoto restaurants (with 花見小路やげんぼり, 出逢ひ茶屋おせん, しぐれ茶屋侘助, 祇をん う桶や う and 花遊小路 江戸川); each cut is prepared one by one so that the texture, flavour and nourishment of beef offal come through. A March 2026 reviewer had eaten the harami bowl at lunch several times before the pandemic. · Per the official site: to overturn the idea of horumon by drawing out its flavour to the limit with careful handwork. · Beef-tongue harihari hot pot with Chinese noodles; harami rice bowl.

places.notes: [Izakaya · Ura-Teramachi, charcoal skewers of fish and pork] A small charcoal-grill izakaya down Ura-Teramachi, with eight counter seats in front of the grill and a tatami room upstairs. The skewers are fish and pork, not chicken: kombu-cured mackerel, oysters with sudachi ponzu, kuruma prawn, and pork rolled round seasonal vegetables — Kujo green onion, shiso, lettuce. The smoked-mackerel macaroni salad is the house's must-order, and the sashimi comes with generous wasabi and ginger. The name, unusual for a cake shop, is that of a grandfather who was a master Noh-costume craftsman. The official site lists a second shop, MATSUNOSUKE N.Y. in Daikanyama, Tokyo, and the book blurb there calls the owner the "Apple Pie Godmother". places.notes: [Bistro · Ayanokoji, meat and wine in a townhouse] A neo-bistro in a townhouse just off the main streets between Karasuma and Kawaramachi — the "29" is niku, meat — with a counter, sofas and some 60 dishes that can all be ordered as halves: smoked mackerel on potato salad, sea urchin pudding with garlic toast, vine-smoked duck, 尾崎牛 beef from Miyazaki, game such as Ezo venison, then a hazelnut crème brûlée. Glass wines from ¥550, mostly French. ¥500 a head cover; most reviewers paid ¥3,000–10,000. Open 17:00–23:00; the site gives Tuesday as closed. Tabelog Bistro 100 2021.
places.chef: Chef (unnamed), trained at hotels in Japan and restaurants in France (Tabelog shop text) · Per the Tabelog shop text: authentic French cooking at fair prices by a chef who trained at renowned hotels in Japan and top restaurants in France, with a focus on meat. Per the official site: the shop first tasted 尾崎牛 at a nearby restaurant, wanted to know more, visited the farm and fell for the beef and its farmer; a counter was built to watch guests react; the wine list, chosen with a sommelier, describes each wine’s region, grape and character; the aim is hospitality that makes guests want to return. Opened 12 July 2011 (Tabelog). Tabelog Bistro "Tabelog 100" 2021. · Per the official site: for a cook, "delicious" is a given; the aim is for guests to want to come back. · Smoked mackerel and potato salad; vine-smoked duck breast; 尾崎牛 grill.
places.gfd: Ask. About 60 dishes, including pasta, gnocchi, quiche, fritters, gratin, bread and cakes alongside grilled meats and carpaccios; portions and dishes can be adjusted on request, but no gluten information is given (official menu; 2026 reviews).
places.vgd: Not vegan in practice: a meat-focused bistro (the "29" in the name means meat); the few vegetable plates are pickles, marinated olives and a bagna cauda (official menu).
places.hours: 17:00–23:00 (last order food 22:30, drinks 23:00) (Tabelog; official site). The official site says closed Tuesday; Tabelog lists every day with irregular closures. places.cu: French restaurant and wine bar with mizutaki (Tabelog) · November 2026 courses: A course with a choice of main ¥9,350; Petit Gourmandises with three glasses of wine ¥16,500; Harmonie Gourmande, six dishes with six 100 ml glasses ¥23,000 (Tabelog, tax and service included) · a September 2026 riverside A course of 9 dishes: purple sweet potato flan with hamo and mushroom clear soup, salad, black wa…
places.notes: [French & wine · Kiyamachi, a riverside platform and a sommelier] A 19-seat French restaurant at the Y-bend of the Takase River where you take off your shoes, sit at the counter or a table, and in summer move out to a platform over the Kamo River facing the Minami-za. The owner is a sommelier, and diners praise the glasses as much as the food: courses run from ¥9,350 (choose your main) to ¥23,000 with six paired glasses. In winter the house turns to mizutaki of Miyama chicken after French starters. Add ¥1,100 table charge and 10% service. Closed Sunday and the 2nd and 4th Monday.
places.chef: Owner-sommelier (unnamed in the sources) · A June 2026 diner spent the evening talking with the owner-sommelier; an October 2026 diner says the owner explains each dish. A September 2026 diner was told the wine list favours second labels of renowned châteaux so that glasses are good without being overly expensive. A diner who has come in the riverside season for about 25 years found the cooking consistently excellent but the prices higher than before (September 2026). Tabelog French WEST "Tabelog 100" 2021. · Seasonal French courses with paired wine; winter mizutaki.
places.gfd: Ask. French courses with bread, sauces such as beurre blanc, a flan and a cutlet, and mizutaki in winter; no gluten information (2025–26 reviews).
places.vgd: Not vegan: the courses centre on wagyu, pork, fish and chicken, and the soups are fish- or chicken-based (2025–26 reviews).

places.hood: Kiyamachi-dori at Dango Bridge, south of Shijo, on the Kamo River — 4 min from Gion-Shijo…
places.cu: Gelato shop of BABBI, the Italian wafer maker with a 70-year history; the gelato uses its wafer pastes, alongside Japanese flavours such as matcha and black sesame (Tabelog) · pistachio, hazelnut, chocolate, ricotta fig, rich milk, salted caramel vanilla, Amaou strawberry, yuzu and lemon, cookies and cream, black sesame, cherry (2024–26 reviews) · cup, wafer or cocoa cone topped with a BABBI wafe…
places.notes: [Gelato · Kiyamachi, Italian gelato over the Kamo River] The only gelato shop of BABBI, the Italian wafer brand, at the Dango Bridge end of Kiyamachi: flavours from pistachio and hazelnut to ricotta fig and Kyoto-leaning matcha and black sesame, in a cup or a cone crowned with a BABBI wafer. Eat inside looking at the river, or from May to October on the riverside platform, where prices run higher (a single was ¥990 there in August 2026). Open daily 13:00–22:00, a handy stop after dinner in Kiyamachi.
places.chef: Shop of the Italian brand BABBI, run in Japan by a company (corporate invoice registrant, Tabelog); no staff named · Per Tabelog (the shop’s own text): a gelato shop from the Italian wafer brand BABBI, which has a 70-year history, using its wafer pastes in the gelato and offering Japanese flavours such as matcha and black sesame; it faces the Kamo River. Walkerplus (February 2020) reported it as the brand’s first gelato shop in Japan; an October 2026 reviewer says it is still the only BABBI location in Japan serving gelato, with ingredients imported from Italy and made in-house, and a September 2026 reviewer notes BABBI also has a Tokyo shop. · Pistachio and hazelnut gelato; wafer-topped cones.
places.gfd: Ask. Gelato comes in a cup or a wafer or cocoa cone topped with BABBI wafer, and the gelato itself uses BABBI’s wafer pastes; no gluten information is published (Tabelog; 2024–26 reviews).
places.vgd: Ask. Most flavours are milk-based (milk, ricotta fig, salted caramel vanilla); fruit flavours such as yuzu and lemon exist, but their ingredients are not published (2024–26 reviews).
places.hours: 13:00–22:00 daily; eat-in and drink last orders 21:30 (Tabelog). places.cu: Teppan counter of Kyoto-style flour dishes (2025–26 reviews) · negiyaki with plenty of green onion, eaten with soy sauce: pork ¥800, mix of beef, pork, squid and chikuwa, extra egg ¥100 · betayaki (thin Kyoto-style okonomiyaki) mix ¥1,000 or beef tendon ¥1,000, with a spicy sauce · okonomiyaki, tonpeiyaki, beef yakisoba, lotus root stuffed with meat, mushrooms, a pizza · special dashimaki rolled …
places.notes: [Negiyaki · Gion, a teppan counter by Yasaka Shrine] A 12-seat counter on Higashioji-dori near Yasaka Shrine, founded in 1984 per a reviewer, where the owner cooks on the teppan in front of you and chats with the regulars along the counter. Order the negiyaki — thin batter under a heap of green onion, with soy sauce (¥800 with pork) — or the Kyoto betayaki with its spicy sauce, and start with the special dashimaki rolled on the griddle with pickled ginger (¥650) while you wait. Book ahead; two-hour limit; cash only. Open until 3:00 on Friday and Saturday; closed Monday.
places.chef: Owner-cook at the teppan (unnamed in the sources) · An October 2026 reviewer gives the founding year as 1984, and another that month calls it a teppan-yaki restaurant with over 40 years of history. Reviewers describe the owner cooking at the teppan and chatting with customers, the owner’s homemade potato salad and simmered whelk, and a counter of regulars. Tabelog Okonomiyaki "Tabelog 100" 2018, 2019, 2022–2025. · Negiyaki; betayaki; dashimaki.

places.cu: Casual izakaya for Kyoto vegetables, obanzai with yuba and nama-fu, Kyoto and Shiga sake, and hot pot (Tabelog) · house hot pot of pork, horumon, asari clams and vegetables in a soy-garlic broth, finished with zosui; also an asari-and-yuba hot pot (2025 reviews) · obanzai: fresh yuba sashimi, fried eggplant in dashi, Manganji peppers, simmered chicken, Kujo green onion, dashimaki tamago; sashimi,…
places.notes: [Izakaya · Pontocho, obanzai and hot pot until 2 am] A large, bright second-floor izakaya on Pontocho with Japanese umbrellas hanging from the ceiling, open from mid-afternoon (noon at weekends) to 2:00 every day: Kyoto obanzai like yuba sashimi and eggplant in dashi, a pork-offal-and-clam hot pot, and Kyoto and Shiga sake, mostly as all-you-can-drink courses (¥5,000–6,000). Easy to book even on the day. Reviews are mixed; many guests are tourists.
places.chef: Operator unnamed in the sources · Opened 1 May 2022 (Tabelog). Per the operator’s Tabelog text: a casual izakaya for first-timers, with seasonal Kyoto vegetables, obanzai such as yuba and nama-fu, and local sake from Kyoto and Shiga. · Obanzai courses; asari and horumon hot pot.
places.gfd: Ask. The house hot pot is soy-sauce based, and the menu includes tempura, sushi and fried eel rolls; no gluten information (2025–26 reviews).
places.vgd: Ask. Tabelog lists vegetarian options and there are yuba, nama-fu and vegetable obanzai, but obanzai such as eggplant in dashi are made with broth, and the hot pot holds pork, offal and clams (Tabelog; 2025–26 reviews).

places.notes: [Yoshoku · south of the Imperial Palace, tonkatsu and seasonal plates] A small, red-carpeted western-style restaurant on Fuyacho run by its owner since 2001 (first an eight-seat counter in Kawaramachi-Sanjo): crisp tonkatsu and creative cutlets, a dense wagyu hamburg steak, beef cutlet and demi-glace stews. Since September 2026 it runs straight through 13:00–21:00 with a one-drink rule; before 15:00 try the Naitou plate (¥2,900, ten a day). Book by phone. Closed Monday.
places.chef: 内藤毅彦 · Owner (店主, official site) · Per the official site: opened in 2001 as an eight-seat, four-tsubo counter at Kawaramachi-Sanjo, when the owner was 33; moved to Yanagibaba-dori south of the palace in 2004 and to Fuyacho-dori in 2019 (December 2019, per Tabelog). From September 2026 the lunch sets ended and the shop switched to straight-through hours. Tabelog Yoshoku WEST "Tabelog 100" 2025. · Tonkatsu; wagyu hamburg steak; Naitou special plate.
places.gfd: Not gluten-free in practice: the menu is built on breaded cutlets (tonkatsu, beef cutlet, ham cutlet, fried shrimp, croquettes), demi-glace stews and curry; no gluten information (official menu; 2026 reviews).
places.vgd: Not vegan: every main is pork, beef, seafood or chicken, and the salads carry house ham, bacon, meatloaf or pork (official menu).
